speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 452, respecting the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company Limited.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the mine and metallurgical plants of Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company Limited are situated astride the Manitoba-Saskatchewan interprovincial boundary adjacent to the town of Flin Flon, Manitoba. The company is the second largest producer of copper and zinc, is one of the larger producers of gold and silver in Canada, and employs at present some 2,200 men. The mining shaft and railway operated by the company run across the interprovincial boundary. The mill, zinc plant and smelter buildings are also situated on both sides of the boundary. While the great majority of the employees are resident in Manitoba and are hired and paid in Manitoba, about one-half of them are working in Saskatchewan and the other half in Manitoba; and in the

Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting
course of their work they move back and forfh daily across the interprovincial boundary.
Throughout the war years, the company's operations were subject in matters of labour relations to P.C. 1003 and to the wage control order. The return of jurisdiction over labour relations and wages and working conditions to the provinces has raised a problem of unique difficulty both to the provinces and to the company with respect to the application of provincial legislation governing labour relations and terms and conditions of employment -notably holidays with pay and hours of work legislation-to the company's operations. This is particularly so as the legislation of the two provinces on these matters is not uniform. In matters of collective bargaining, neither the company nor the union are in a position to bargain with certainty on matters relating to terms and conditions of employment in view of the doubt and. difficulties as to application of provincial legislation.
The company has discussed the question with the governments of both Manitoba and Saskatchewan and with the Department of Labour in Ottawa, and also made a submission within the last week to the industrial relations committee of this house.
Manitoba and Saskatchewan, who are the only provinces interested in this matter, have requested that, with a view to meeting the admitted difficulties of the situation, the dominion should be asked to enact legislation to bring these mining operations of the company within the scope of dominion jurisdiction. Both governments have agreed on the procedure to be followed to effect this result, namely:
(a)	That parliament should declare these mining operations of the company to be works for the advantage of two or more provinces.
(b)	To provide that the rates of pay, hours of work and other terms and conditions of employment of employees of the company employed upon such undertaking shall be such as are established in collective agreements entered into from time to time between the company and the representatives of its employees but without affecting the application of provincial workmen's compensation *legislation.
The unions representing employees of the company support the company's representations and the foregoing proposals.
This bill is being proceeded with at this session and as the difficulties relating to the company's operations are represented by the company and by the provincial governments as requiring an early solution, the government decided it best to introduce this bill

which gives effect to the request of the two provinces mentioned and the representations made by the company to the industrial relations committee of this house. I believe that members of this house will be in agreement and be prepared to support the provisions of the bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I have just one observation to make, and that is with regard to bills which come from Westminster to the dominions. There is a particular way of drafting them, and when they are passed at Westminster ip certain language they are supposed to be passed by the dominion in exactly the same language. I consider this plain red tape, and I will tell you why. The title does not affect the king as king of Canada; it affects him only as former emperor of India. Because the description of His Majesty the King of Great Britain as emperor of India is changed, I do not see why we should pass a bill like this, which does not concern us any more than a change in the name of the Dominion of Canada would affect the people of India. This is only to give us the illusion that we have something to do with that business. We 'have nothing to do with it. What is done concerning India does not concern Canada any more than what is done in Canada affects India, with the exception of trade relations.

TRUST COMPANIES ACT VARIOUS amendments
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 417 to amend the Trust Companies Act.
He said: This bill contains a number of rather technical amendments to the Trust Companies Act. There has been no substantial amendment of that act since I think 1923 or 1924, and the trust companies who operate under dominion charter have discussed with the superintendent of insurance and with myself certain amendments which they felt it was desirable to make to the act in order to bring it up to date.
I can outline very briefly the principal amendments. First, they authorize an increase in the number of directors a company may have from twenty-one to thirty. The bill will permit the naming of an executive committe of the board of directors if desired. If these trust companies so desire they may have their capital divided into shares of $10 each instead of $100, which is consistent with the change made in the Bank Act at the last revision. There are provisions relating to the books of the company and transfers of stock, to bring them into line with the corresponding provisions of the Companies Act. There is an extension of the period for holding real estate other than office premises from seven to twelve years. The investment powers of trust companies are brought more nearly into conformity with those of Canadian life insurance companies under the insurance act. There are sundry minor amendments but those are the principal amendments to the act. The bill is now before the house.

I rise merely to make a suggestion to the minister with respect to this bill. As the minister has properly pointed out, the bill contains a number of technical amendments to the Trust Companies Act. Personally I think, and the

Mr. Chairman, while the hon. members admit quite readily that the acting Minister of Mines and Resources can meet fully the demands of his numerous duties, I am sure that we all deplore the absence of our very good friend the Hon. Mr. Glen, Minister of Mines and Resources. May I express the hope that Providence will vouchsafe him every possible solace as well as recovery from his present illness.
I have listened most attentively to the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). While agreeing with him on several points, I must say that I have clearly stated in the past my position with regard to immigration, and if I rise this morning it is not for the purpose of adding much to what I have already said, but rather to reaffirm the stand I took in former debates.
In order to please my hon. friends, I say at once that I shall not take more than a few minutes.
Hear, hear.

I have in my hand the speech delivered on May 1, 1947, by the prime minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) where I notice a sentence I fully endorse and which should ever remain in the minds of those who advocate immigration:
The government will seek by legislation, regulation, and vigorous administration, to ensure
Supply-Mines and Resources

the careful selection and permanent settlement of such numbers of immigrants as can advantageously be absorbed in our national economy.
Hear, hear.

To my mind, that stand is the most logical and worthy of the leader of a national economy like ours. I believe it is the soundest position that could be taken: "such numbers ... as can advantageously be absorbed in our national economy".
Hear, hear.

I have
already said, and I now repeat, that I am not in favour of mass immigration. I admit that a certain movement of people can take place between the various countries over a number of years, but I would not like the government to bring here too many immigrants some of whom will stay on the lands where they will apparently have settled down, while a greater number, perhaps, will take up residence in cities where they will merely increase the number of unemployed and lengthen what is commonly and quite appropriately called the bread-line, should this country have the misfortune of going through a period of unemployment.
I agree with the statement which the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) made not very long ago when he said', in answer to those who believe that we have an unlimited area of tillable soil, that the land awaiting cultivation may not be as extensive as it is claimed to be.
That's right.

Having carefully considered this important matter of Canadian immigration, it is, to my mind, clearly shown that even though the area of Canada is greater than that of the United States whose population numbers 130,000,000 inhabitants, we cannot state that the tillable land in the country is as extensive as is claimed in certain quarters.
From 1871 to 1937, we admitted a very large number of immigrants. This morning, I added a few figures, and I find that 5,234,235 immigrants have come to Canada. Of that number, a certain percentage remained on the land. Incidentally, I must say that when the Immigration Branch gives instructions to its officials in European countries with reference to the choice of immigrants, it should stress .that they select first candidates who intend to settle on the farm and apply regulations obliging them to remain on the land
Five years.

Five years, as suggested1 by the hon. member for Resti-gouehe-Madawaska, would not be too long and would allow us to determine whether those who left farms in Europe really intended to settle on the land and1 become bona fide farmers, or whether they planned to remain there only until they could leave to swell the city population.
That's right.

If we take the trouble of establishing the percentage relating to population in urban and rural centres, we will find that, generally speaking, especially in my province, the advantage seems to be in favour of the cities.
Always.

According to a survey, there are more people in the cities of the province of Quebec, than in the country. If we want our farmers to supply as much food as possible to the city workers, we must see that the proportion again favours our rural areas.
Hear, hear.

That is why, during a debate last year-if I may be permitted to refer to it for a moment-I advocated a programme of reconstruction, comprising the setting up of recreational and educational centres in our rural communities, a programme that should be partly financed by the provinces and partly by the dominion government. Unfortunately, agreement with the provinces, especially Quebec and Ontario, is too slow to come about, so that our rural communities cannot benefit as much as they would wish to from those agreements, and specially from the financial assistance of which they could avail themselves to finance those rural and educational centres and render them far more interesting and attractive, in order to instil into our young people love for the land and for rural communities in general.
Coming back to the question of immigration, I have here a document, which was laid on the table of the house, showing, as I mentioned a while ago, that 5,234,235 people immigrated to Canada between 1871 and 1937. I agree that we Should accept a certain number of immigrants. The Right Hon. the Prime Minister stated on May 1, 1947, that Canada had attempted to alleviate the sufferings of nations that had been sorely tried during the war, especially in Europe. Canada has largely contributed to the alleviation of tht sufferings of people grouped in displaced persons camps, and continues to do so. It should

Supply-Mines and Resources
not be assumed, however, that Canada will do everything single-handed' and without the help of the other nations of the world. I repeat that only a reasonable policy, such as was outlined by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King in this bouse on May 1, where he stated that we must first ascertain the number of immigrants that our economy can absorb-such a policy is the only one which will prevent us from reverting to the unfortunate condition that prevailed during the last depression, a recurrence of which is always possible, of seeing immigrants who had settled on farms or accepted employment in plants or industrial concerns, swell what we used to call the "bread-line". Therefore, we should not accept any more than our national economy can absorb.
I agree with those who are conversant with the problem of immigration that we could accept a certain number of immigrants, and that a certain natural movement can take place between the various countries of the world in the course of years. Some are complaining about the loss of talented young people and a certain number are evidently leaving Canada for the United States.
I notice that every time the subject of immigration is discussed and particularly when mention is made of the fact that we need a greater number of British immigrants, nobody ever stops to consider the great economic difficulties which are experienced by the United Kingdom at the present time. Under the title "Friday Forum-Europe offers good immigrants", here is what Mr. M. J. Heffernan wrote in the Montreal Gazette of July 11th, 1947:
(Text):
Europe Offers Good Immigrants
The fundamental fact is that Canada is losing several thousands of her most skilled farmers and tens of thousands of her trained youth. If the dominion is not to grow anaemic new blood must be had, and the source is immigration.
(Translation):
These people never seem to think that even without immigration-and I speak for my own province-we may place our hopes in the large families which are the pride of Canadian motherhood. Even without mass immigration, we may rest assure that the natural growth of population will give us the men to sow our land with wheat, so that the stems, rustling softy in the breeze, may sing of a people's hope to live in spite of everything.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Heffernan continues-
(Text):
For the thousands who are leaving Canada there are millions in Europe eager to come, anxious to escape from the miseries of war, and willing to build up, where Canadians will give them the chance, the lives they have snatched from slave labour and internment camps.
(Translation):
Counter arguments are often put forward. When -the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) dared to bring a few Polish girls to Canada to work at his plant, many unfortunate things were said in this house. Some went so far as to accuse -the hon. member for Beauce of exploiting what is called "slave labour" in Europe. As I was saying before I started quoting this report, we are prone to forget the problems of British economy. It seems to me that we are rendering poor service to the United Kingdom when we persist in bringing to Canada, by hundreds of thousands-the quota has been set at 600,000 -farmers and workers who are absolutely needed in Great Britain at this time for the reconstruction and the rehabilitation of the British Isles.
Hear, hear.

I have here the June 24 issue of the magazine World Report. I find in it a picture showing a poster held by English workers during a demonstration. This poster reads:
(Text):
We need 40,000 more miners in the United Kingdom. We need 75,000 more textile workers in the United Kingdom. We need 40,000 more farm workers.
They need these in the United Kingdom and we are asking them to send hundreds of thousands of immigrants to Canada. We are asking them to do that at a time when they need so much farm help, so many textile workers and so many coal miners?
(Translation):
I believe there is a much more reasonable and patriotic way of helping the United Kingdom than by asking it to pinch and scrape in order that our population be increased. Besides, I would request my hon. friends, supporters of mass immigration, to cast a sympathetic eye on the United Kingdom which, unfortunately, cannot rely on natural population increase, while we can count on that factor, especially in the province of Quebec and even in the other provinces.

Hear, hear!

Supply-Mines and Resources

I claim that it is a great pity to request it to make an excessive effort and force it, as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) said last night, to import workers from other European countries in an effort to make up for the century-old inadequacy of the birth rate and the scarcity of workers which the very able socialist government is attempting to put to work in the British Isles. It seems to me that the fact of demanding that the present situation of Canada be taken into account, of asking who is now doing more than his share, who has done more than his share during the war, who. has, in spite of the three, four or five great powers, joined the council of nations and of insisting that our country be not asked to do more than the others, is not acting as a bad Canadian.
When British immigrants are requested, I hope I shall not sound a flat note in asking that consideration be given to the sons of old France and intrepid Belgium who wish to come to Canada to live among those they consider almost as brothers.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wished to restate very clearly my precise attitude on this most ticklish and complex matter of immigration.
I repeat that my words are not to be construed as meaning that I favour closing our frontiers to all immigration. Every time I speak on national problems in this house, I endeavour to express . views that are as essentially Canadian as possible. I do not wish to close to those who have faith in the future of Canada a door which they would throw wide open, but I want those who advocate immigration, to realize that our economy so badly shaken up by the war must not be jeopardized and that, in the near future, we may have to support people who will claim jobs from us, a larger number of whom, possibly, will be among those who have entered our country more or less recently rather than among those whose ancestors have lived here for years and even centuries.

Mr. J. E. MATTHEWS .(Brandon): I want to offer a few remarks in connection with these estimates, and I may as well do so now as under the item to which it more fittingly belongs, that for national parks and historic sites. I want to urge particularly that funds be made available from somewhere for the further development this year of our international peace garden at Manitoba and in North Dakota. I can easily understand that there is not at the moment a very live IMr. Michaud.]
interest in this parliament concerning that project. It was one of those undertakings which were laid aside during the war; then when the war ended it was found that to a large extent a new generation of parliamentarians occupied seats in this chamber, and few of them knew anything about the aims and work of this organization, officially known as International Peace Garden Incorporated.
I am very sorry that the Minister of Mines and Resources is not in his place in the chamber in these days, and I am sure that one and all are hoping that the rest he is now enjoying may bring him back to a complete restoration of health. We are fortunate, however, that his duties are being undertaken by a gentleman who is also one of broad outlook and of undoubted capacity. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, and because the Canadian government is in honour bound committed to the furtherance of this undertaking, I desire as a matter of information to place on the record a brief, but I trust a clear, resume of the garden's background. I should emphasize that which is already suggested, that it is not a municipal, a provincial or even a national undertaking; it is international in every sense of the word. The seed was sown away back in 1929 when an international convention of the Gardeners Association of North America was held in Toronto, the first time that important association had ever met in Canada. At that convention the idea of a peace garden was submitted by the late Henry J. Moore of Islington, Ontario. Mr. Moore, as some hon. members are aware, was not an amateur gardener but a professional one of wide repute, a writer of recognized ability and a valued member of the Royal Horticultural Society of London, England. He was a man whose ability, vision, and experience were widely recognized. I am under the impression that he served for many years as horticultural expert for the Ontario government. In an inspiring address at the Toronto convention Mr. Moore won his way into the hearts of all his hearers as he suggested the laying out of a magnificent garden at some point on the international line as a beautiful and living memorial to everlasting peace, and an appealing symbol of good will between our two nations. Reading at this time, eighteen, years after it was given, a summary of Mr.. Moore's oration, for such I may call it, one cannot fail to be impressed by the similarity of thought, the expression of idealism and the cogency of appeal existing between that speech and the one delivered in this house a few weeks ago by President Truman.

Supply-Mines and Resources
Mr. Moore in the course of his Toronto speech made this announcement :
The United States ambassador to Canada, Hon. William Phillips, the highest representative of the American government, and the Governor General of Canada, Lord Willingdon, the direct representative of the King and of Great Britain, have in letters with the words of statesmen and of Christian gentlemen endorsed the project. The Prime Minister of Canada, the Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King kindly sent a representative to this meeting. The Hon. George S. Henry, a minister of the Ontario government, is present. The Hon. John S. Martin, Minister of Agriculture of Ontario, and the Hon. William Motherwell of the dominion government are in accord with the project. What better endor-sation is possible?
Mr. Moore's proposal was carried unanimously and with wide acclaim, so wide that in a short time no less than fifty-six national, state and provincial organizations forwarded pledges of their support. These pledges, many of which came from the middle west and southern states, were sponsored by such organizations as the Canadian and American Red Cross societies, the Women's Federal Institute of Canada; the Imperial Order, Daughters of the Empire, both in Canada and in the United States; the Canadian business and professional women's club, the Manitoba and North Dakota chapter of the order of the Eastern Star and came from many western Canadian municipal- ^ ities, boards of trade, school boards and even from many of the scholars themselves. Read that list, Mr. Chairman, and you will find the names of some of the most prominent people on this continent, although a few of them have now passed on. This general committee having been chosen, no time was lost in appointing a committee to select a site, and no restriction was imposed upon that committee geographically or otherwise. If you want to grasp the idea of internationalism, listen to the names of those who composed that site committee: H. J. Moore of Toronto, Joseph Dunlop of South Euclid, Ohio, Robert P. Brydon of Cleveland, Ohio. Many sites were inspected along the boundary, but eventually one was unanimously chosen in the Turtle mountains, a range of hills situated astride the boundary between Manitoba and North Dakota. Those hills, at one time-heavily timbered, rise to a height of 2,500 feet-above sea level. They extend forty-five miles east and west and twenty miles north and south. They were named by the Indians centuries before the coming of the white man. At a later meeting of those interested, held not in Canada but at Asbury Park, New Jersey, on September 17, 1931, the Turtle-mountain site received unanimous endorsation. The area of the garden consists of 2,340 acres, 1,452 acres in Canada, donated by the Manitoba government, and 888 acres on the United States side, donated partly by Washington and partly by the state of North Dakota. The selection of this site was greatly facilitated by the Hon. D. G. McKenzie, at that time Minister of Mines and Natural Resources in the Manitoba government, who on behalf of that government offered to donate the generous acreage I have just stated. Over much of this area there is a profusion of flowered foliage and an abundance of wild life, particularly bird life. Potentially it is one of those rare locations where the harmony and colour of the flowers symbolize that harmony of ideals which has enabled two great peoples to live side by side in friendship and understanding for almost one hundred and fifty years.

It is interesting to recall a paragraph of the speech from the throne at the opening of the Manitoba legislature on February 29, 1932, under the leadership of Hon. John Bracken, always an ardent supporter of the garden:
A memorable event of the past year is the provision made for the peace garden in the Turtle mountain region of Manitoba and North Dakota. This international project ought to have a prominent place in the peace *chronicles of the present era when every thinking person in the world is compelled to realize that one of the most_ important questions facing our civilization is that of world peace, friendship, and cooperation.
I recall also an editorial of that time in the Winnipeg Tribune, from which I quote:
It is a worthy, a splendid project, and one that has the enthusiastic approval not only of the people of Manitoba and Western Canada, but of other millions in both countries... Some of the most magnificent monuments in the world have been erected to commemorate lost causes, vanished glories and ruined hopes. A peace garden, let us hope, will symbolize in its own living beauty, ever more cordial relations between the two countries.
I was privileged, Mr. Chairman, in having been one of almost 50,000 persons who were present at the official opening of that garden on July 24, 1932. People were assembled there from great distances in the central west, Americans and Canadians, many of whom not so long before had lost loved ones on the battlefields of Europe. But it mattered not whether American or Canadian, we were there as one people, our hearts and minds bent on one purpose. I have never forgotten the hush that prevailed over that great .multitude during the unveiling of a huge cairn of native stone erected right astride the boundary line. Upon that cairn was a bronze plaque bearing this inscription:	"To God in His Glory we two
nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as 'long as men shall live we will not take up arms against one another."
Those seeds of international fidelity, sown years ago, came to early fruition when only seven years later our two nations found themselves fighting side by side in the most destructive war in all history. For us to have been fighting on opposite sides is simply unthinkable.
Even prior to this official opening elaborate plans of development had been prepared. These plans were approved-and I want you to note this-by the natural parks service of the United States and by the national parks bureau of Canada. The project was so designed that the total area controlled by International Peace Garden Incorporated will form one harmonious unit. These approved plans have already been developed to a considerable *extent, including landscaping, permanent fenc-

ing, highway building and the opening of branch roads in the park area. However, during the war only 'maintenance work was carried on on the Canadian side by the Manitoba government. The time has now arrived when the work already done can be conserved only by hurrying more of those plans to completion. This further work is the responsibility of the federal government. Why do I make that statement? First, because the whole proposal is international in its aspect; also because the dominion government has already expended through the province of Manitoba approximately $52,000, and has supplemented this by substantial supplies of material to the United States side from Riding Mountain national park.
The United States section was developed very largely by the civilian conservation corps previous to Pearl Harbor, and a customs and immigration station is to be erected at a cost of $60,000, while the state of North Dakota has appropriated more than $30,000 for the development of the United States section. I have to confess that up to date there has been much more development on the United States side than on the Canadian. After a standstill during the war I understand the United States directors have recently made representations to the United States government for the early resumption of financial assistance, which will no doubt be granted.
May I make clear the fact that the international peace garden is incorporated under the laws of Manitoba and North Dakota, and has been recognized by both Canadian and United States governments. By that recognition Canada has given her approval, which, as I said, prior to the outbreak of the war was backed by repeated contributions. I am confident that our American friends will find Canada will not break faith in her continued support of this project. Henry J. Moore, that great Canadian, has passed to his reward. Strangely enough his death took place on September 21, 1946, the day of the last annual meeting of the association he had founded and always held so dear. He and many other enthusiastic sponsors of the plan have thrown the torch to younger hands, and I want to pay tribute to the manner in which the present directors have carried on from year to year without a dollar of remuneration, simply as a labour of love and out of allegiance to a great ideal; carried on with patience and understanding in the face of many difficulties. Seven of the present directors are Americans from various states, while eight are Canadians from different parts of western Canada. I know most of those fifteen directors,

Since this project, so far as the federal government is concerned, has been a forgotten responsibility since 1940, I want t.o go on record as having now placed before the dominion parliament a resume of this idealistic undertaking, and to make the request, that in preparing the estimates for succeeding years reasonably substantial amounts be included definitely for that work. Other memorials that we may call peace memorials have been erected in past years at great expense between the nations of Canada and the United States, such as the peace bridge between Fort Erie and Buffalo, which was built at a cost of some
85.000,000, the Ambassador bridge between Windsor and Detroit, the bridge between Sarnia and Port Huron and the Ivy Lea bridge at the Thousand Islands. They are all large and ambitious undertakings, and in addition to serving commercial purposes they constitute a good example of the good neighbour policy. But let me point out that all these are in Ontario and relatively only a few miles apart. May I suggest further that there are provinces other than Ontario, and states other than New York, where the citizens desire to give some expression of the fact that they too live in equality and mutual respect. As far as I can recall this garden is the only peace memorial along the international boundary, from the bridges I have mentioned to the Pacific coast, a distance of over two thousand miles. Its further development on the part of Canada will express our practical reaction to the recent statement of President Truman in this chamber:
We intend to cooperate actively and loyally with all who honestly seek, as we do, to build a better world in which mankind can live in peace and prosperity. We count Canada in the forefront of those who share these objectives and ideals. With such friends we face the future unafraid.
Someone will say this is simply another call for more expenditure. That may be, but there are some expenditures, even governmental, that prove to be good investments. That is Canada's experience in regard to the tourist industry. Our revenue from that source in 1946 amounted to the handsome sum of $227,000,000. I am confident that in the next few years a tremendous expansion is possible in that industry. Therefore I desire to point out that the international peace garden is located on perhaps the most important highway connecting central United States and central Canada. Someone has called it the main street of America, coming as it does directly from central America, Mexico and the central states and entering Canada via the peace garden, thence continuing northward almost in a direct line to Riding Mountain national park, on to The Pas, soon to Churchill and perhaps in time to the shores of Hudson Bay, at all events going through vast areas of wild and primitive scenery in our great northwest. Tourist development in Canada is simply astounding in its possibilities. I may mention Riding Mountain national park as an illustration. It was practically unknown a few years ago but led every national pairk in Canada with the exception of one in the number of visitors last year, and without exception led every park in the number of automobiles entering the park area in 1946. People went there in droves from every state in the union and every province in Canada. Most of us know something of the excellence and wide circulation of the Christian Science Monitor, which is published in the United States. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there has been no collusion in this matter; but the reading room received this morning- and word was passed on to me-the latest issue of that publication, which contains almost a full page illustrative of Riding Mountain national park. I would advise every hon member of this house to read this article and look at the illustrations, so that, as far as the tourist industry is concerned, we may come to see ourselves as others see us.
More and more will United States tourists be drawn northward by the magnetic attraction of our natural parks. We all know how lasting are first impressions, whether favourable 'or unfavourable. Therefore when these tourists reach the front door of Canada we want them to be greeted, not by frowning fort nor silent sentry, but by a smiling garden symbolic of a peace so permanent that, like "the glory of the garden it shall never pass away".

May I emphasize in conclusion the intriguing fact that instead of being in the far east or in the distant west this garden is located actually within thirty miles of the exact centre of the North American continent. Surely that is a fitting place for a tall and commanding peace tower, proclaiming to the world the friendship between our two nations. I suggest further that the time may come, perhaps sooner than we think, when in that parklike garden in that unique centre of an expansive continent, there may be erected a joint statue of our two national war leaders, President Roosevelt and Prime Minister King who, having given superb leadership in the days of peace, yet rose to greatest heights in the hour of their country's greatest danger.

Just before the hon. member resumes his seat I should like to ask him a question. I wonder if it has been brought to his attention that the Waterton Lakes national park in southwestern Alberta was made an international peace park several years ago. That really should go on record in modification of what the hon. member has said.

The debate we have had this morning on this department lends force to what I wish to say at this point. The Department of Mines and Resources has now become a receptacle for various tag ends of government business. It deals with Indian affairs, national parks, immigration, mines and resources and, apparently, national memorials. I want to make a plea to the minister, and since he is a practical man I feel he will agree, that this department should be what it says it is; that is, a department of mines and resources. This morning we have had a discussion on immigration, national parks and national memorials, and as I see it the debate on the minister's estimates will cover a large and varied number of unrelated subjects. Next to agriculture the development of the natural resources of this country should be the most productive endeavour of any government. I am prepared to say that within a very few years production from our natural resources, our mines and forests, will be of greater value to this country than agriculture owing to the growing importance of mineral production. I would ask the government to consider during the recess removing Indian affairs and immigration from the Department of Mines and Resources. As we have seen here today, immigration should be a matter for the Secretary of State or for some other department-I suggest the Secretary of State,

who deals with naturalization. As we have seen this morning, it is a subject in which both races in Canada are interested. It is a subject which interests the whole of Canada. It may be suggested that it calls for a separate department. Certainly it is not an appropriate subject for the consideration of the Minister of Mines and Resources, who should be a practical man, preferably an engineer.
I come now to Indian affairs, and here again I suggest that the Secretary of State's department is the proper one to take over the Indian Affairs branch.	By no stretch of the
imagination can Indian affairs be considered as having anything to do with mines and resources. The Indian affairs committee has met this session, as it did last session, and if I am correct it has produced, apart from the veterans affaire committee, the most voluminous report that has ever been brought down in any parliament in Canada. The report covers many thousands of pages of evidence. For the Minister of Mines and Resources to have to concern himself with such voluminous reports is not in the best interests of the country.
This brings me to the complaint I have about the whole policy of this government and the other governments with regard to mines and resources. I am not going to go into fiscal policies or anything of the kind, but it has been shown that the money spent by the government on the development of our mines, on geological surveys, on laboratories, has been a mere fraction of one per cent of the total federal budget. If we are ever to have a balanced economy as between agriculture on the one hand and mining and forests on the other, as between imports and exports, we shall have to do far more than we have done in the direction of developing our mines.
The majority of the people do not realize what a serious situation confronts the mining industry today, particularly gold mining. Prices and costs have risen and are still rising steadily. The product has been artificially reduced in price by government action, and reduced to a very serious degree.
Last week the International Nickel Company agreed to a further increase of 13% cents an hour to its workers. We have reached this state in Canada today, that if that increase is to be imposed on the gold mines also it will be the death knell of gold mining in this country. The industry- at the present time is just getting by. There may be flurries in the market; expansive statements may be, made by certain people in the industry and by promoters, but the basic -thing is that the cost of producing an ounce of gold is steadily

Supply-Mines and Resources
rising whereas the price received for an ounce of gold has -been artificially reduced. When these two meet, as they are nearly doing now, then mining ends. I shall have something to say about that on the estimates of the Minister of Finance, but since this is an administration item I take this occasion to say that it is imperative that the Department of Mines and Resources should be what it professes to be, a department dealing with the development. of mines and the natural resources of the country. If it is not, if it is, as I have said, the national w'aste paper basket into which every unwanted and difficult problem is thrown, then we shall have a headless organization which will have no direction and which will be incapable of functioning efficiently. One has only to consider the fact. I have mentioned, that a mere fraction of one per cent of the federal budget is spent on the development of natural resources.
I do not know whether he is the new minister, but the right hon. gentleman who is responsible for the department- at the present time, an industrialist, a man who understands chains of command and who understands that to work efficiently a department must deal with one or two basic subjects, must realize that the main function of his department must not get sidetracked. I do hope that in the recess the reorganization of the Department of Mines and Resources will be undertaken. In this I am supported by the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, whose brief several years ago was one of the most cogent advocacies of the policy I now recommend to the minister.

It is regrettable that owing to the government's inadequate immigration policy so many debates have been forced on the house on the subject of immigration. During the last two years I myself have spoken on this subject no fewer than six times and with the present inadequate immigration provisions my conscience would not be clear if I did not say something on this item today.
In the July 8 issue of the Toronto Daily Star I find a report to the effect that the Deputy Minister of Mines and Resources, Dr. H. L. Keenleyside, had stated:
The Canadian seeking to have h-is displaced acquaintance brought to Canada need not be a relative but must accept responsibility for the immigrant.
And farther down:
He said it was a matter of government policy whether further displaced persons would be accepted immediately.
It was believed, however, that further displaced persons would be allowed entry prior
to Canada's agreement with the intergovernmental committee on refugees to take a quota yet to be agreed upon.
Such statements appearing in the press have confused the people, and many of them have been writing to me asking whether an order in council has been passed providing for the admission to Canada of persons other than relatives. So far I have not seen an order in council to that effect, and I assume that the statement made some time ago by the Minister of Mines and Resources contained the complete provisions so far as immigration is concerned. I understand that only the following persons can be brought into Canada from displaced persons camps:
1.	An agriculturist having sufficient means to farm in Canada.
2.	An agriculturist entering Canada to farm, when destined to a father, father-in-law, son, son-in-law, brother, brother-in-law, uncle or nephew engaged in agriculture as his principal occupation, who is in a position to receive such immigrant and establish him on a farm.
3.	A farm labourer entering Canada to engage in assured farm employment.
4.	A person experienced in mining, lumbering or logging, entering Canada to engage in assured employment in any one of such industries.
5.	The husband or wife, the son, the daughter, the brother or sister together with husband or wife and unmarried children, if any; the father or mother, the orphan nephew or niece under 21 years of age of any person legally resident in Canada who is in a position to receive and care for such relatives. The term "orphan" used in this clause means a child bereaved of both parents.
6.	A person entering Canada for the purpose of marriage to a legal resident thereof, provided that the prospective husband is able to maintain his intended wife.
When the minister speaks I should like him to state whether the government has passed any order in council extending the provisions which I have placed on the record. I should like to know also the present immigration provisions so far as displaced persons and refugees are concerned. We should have a clarification of the government's immigration policy, because I hope we shall all be going home soon and our constituents will be asking for information. I should be grateful if the minister would give us the required information.
Before proceeding with the few remarks I wanted to make I should like to pay a tribute to the senate committee on immigra-

tion and labour for the splendid1 work it has done in connection with immigration during the past two sessions. That committee has done more for immigration than any other body in the way of arousing public opinion and prodding the government to adopt the .measures which it has adopted so far. I am somewhat disturbed when I read that the United States of America is considering admitting 400,000 displaced persons and refugees; that the United Kingdom has taken a large number and is taking many more; that Argentina is picking the cream of the material available; that Brasil has accepted quite a number and is continuing to take more, and that Australia has also taken quite a number and is still taking more-what about Canada?
The. arguments used by the immigration authorities are that there are no transportation facilities available. All who have had cases referred to them by their constituents and people in other parts of Canada know that very few immigrants can qualify under the present regulations. It seems to me the time has come when we should change the controls and permit a number of intellectuals to come in.
The government seems to be afraid of people with brains; all they are interested in is people with muscle. If muscle is all we want, we can bring in a bunch of horses, but of course horses would not pay taxes and they could not vote and that would be a disadvantage. If we are interested only in physical strength and not in individuals as such, then the government should bring in horses. I know a gentleman in Sudbury who is well off financially. He has two or three cousins in displaced persons camps in Europe and he wants to bring them to Canada. He has bought two or three quarters of land and has given up the bakery business in which he was engaged. He is willing to provide any guarantee the government wants in order to permit him to bring these people in. What is the answer? "We are sorry, but your cousins are, first, a newspaper man and not a farmer and therefore he does not qualify and, second, a lawyer."
May I ask a question?
The hon. gentleman can ask his question when I get through.

We are in committee, and if the hon. gentleman wishes to ask me any

questions later I shall be only too glad to answer them. I have in the neighbourhood of 2,000 applications from people all over Canada for assistance to bring in relatives. Most of these intellectuals are willing to work on farms; that is what they want to do when they arrive here. They do not want to pursue their professions which they followed before the war because many of them at least have not a sufficiently good command of the English language. Surely, Mr. Chairman, if these men want to come in, and they are with us in every sense and are the best material we can get, we should let them come in.
I have always pleaded for displaced persons and refugees regardless of their racial origin, but I wish to place on the record a special plea for sympathetic consideration for persons of Ukrainian origin. On checking over a table which was presented by Mr. Jolliffe, the director of immigration, on Wednesday, April 30, 1947, I find that among those admitted to Canada-these are European, not British immigrants-there were 216 Czechoslovakians, 844 Germans, 627 Poles, 28 Roumanians, 23 Russians, and so on down the list, but only one Ukrainian. I should like the minister to tell me why this discrimination existed. Is it because they feel the people of Ukrainian origin have not stood by them well enough in the past? I must say that they did. People of Ukrainian origin have supported the party in power today more than any other party in Canada, and yet this is the consideration they get- only one Ukrainian admitted in the twelve months of 1946.

That is true, but travelling in Europe I found the situation was similar in all the zones, British and French, except the Soviet zone, about which we know less.
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to a few figures in the. table. Of those repatriated from the end of the war to December 15, 1946, only 2'5 per cent of Estonians were repatriated back to their homeland, which is now controlled by the Soviets; Latvians, 2-6 per cent; Lithuanians, -7 per cent-not even one out of a hundred was repatriated. Now I come to Poles. Hon. members will find a footnote in the table which says that of the 116,144 Poles in camp, 51,640 are Polish Ukrainians, which simply means Ukrainians, but the Poles held that territory after the first great war and prior to the second great war. What are the figures there? Remember that the majority of these people called Polish are Ukrainians; 67-3 per cent of them were repatriated by various means, including force. Now I come to Russians, which largely means Ukrainians who were under the Soviet union prior to September 1, 1939. There were 98-1 per cent of them repatriated.
I come to Yugoslavs, of whom 79'8 per cent were repatriated; stateless, none; others and unclaimed, 86-i per cent; Jews, no per cent. I claim that on the basis of these figures those against whom such tremendous force was applied to repatriate them, the Ukrainians, should be given the preference in admittance to Canada. The reason is that under the Yalta agreement between Britain, the United States and the Soviet union it was agreed that persons who resided in territories held by Soviets prior to September 1, 1939, should be repatriated to the Soviet union without regard to their personal wishes and by force if necessary. That applies chiefly to Ukrainians. Take, for instance, a Ukrainian who is a Ukrainian and not a Russian, and who has never been a communist, but resided in the part of the Ukraine that prior to the war was held by the Soviet union. Perhaps he expressed himself against communism and was imprisoned, or he may just have returned from a prison camp in Siberia and now finds himself in a displaced persons camp. What happens? The British and United States authorities say: We must repatriate you-you must go back to your country. That means death or the concentration camp-nothing else.
I appreciate the efforts of this government, particularly of the Minister of National Health

and Welfare for his stand on this question before the united nations. This world is supposed to be civilized, and when people say that they want to remain Christians and democrats, that they want to cling to the western world, we should not say to them: Your crime is that you are against communism and therefore you must go back under the Soviets.
I have no time to review the conditions under which these people have been and still are being repatriated. I am sorry to have to say this but there is one man in the United States, a former mayor of New York, Mr. LaGuardia, for whom not one tear will be shed by the displaced persons when he passes away because he favoured men retaining positions in displaced persons camps who were definitely pro-communist. Many who showed any consideration for displaced persons were put out. In this day and age, when we claim to have such high ideals about humanity and use all the high sounding words, we should review our own conscience and see whether we can improve on what we have been doing. Time does not allow me to put on the record before the noon recess everything that I have to say but I pointed out at the outset that the government offers as an excuse that there are no transportation facilities available. That is fine; I recognize the problem to a certain extent, but let me point out this to the committee. In the Daily Tribune of Toronto of June 24, 1947, a communist publication, I read this announcement on page 7:
One hundred and ten Canadians going to youth fete in Prague.
Over thirty members of the national federation of labor youth will attend the world youth festival at Prague, Czechoslovakia, next month, it was announced here to-day by federation officials.
Thirty members will come from all parts of Canada and will represent trade unions, cultural organizations from many language groups, and progressive youth community clubs.
The N.F.L.Y. delegation will be part of a 110-strong Canadian delegation from a large number of organizations being sent under the auspices of the Canadian committee of the world federation of democratic youth. Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 451, respecting the refunding and adjustment of indebtedness of the four western provinces to the government of Canada in respect of certain outstanding loans for relief and other purposes and final settlement of the claims of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in respect of natural resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is designed to authorize a definitive settlement of certain claims and counterclaims existing between the government of Canada on the one hand and the governments of western provinces on the other hand.
It will be recalled that the impact of the depression of the thirties was most devastating in the case of western Canada. Unemploy^-ment and low prices were the common lot of all Canada, but to the west, an economy built on a highly specialized grain growing industry, there came the additional scourge of a succession of drought years, aggravating enormously the economic losses and multiplying the problems and the financial burdens of government.
While the expenditures of the provincial governments increased many times, their .revenues dropped precipitately, creating deficits of a very large order. Taxes were increased and new levies were imposed, but such action did not go far to bridge the deficits. Even for governments in the soundest financial position, it is usually not easy to borrow at reasonable rates, but so great had been the economic disaster to western Canada that the credit of provincial governments resting upon that agricultural economy was seriously impaired or in danger of being lost altogether. In the late thirties, the improvement in economic conditions and in the investment market was more than offset by the huge debts which the western provinces had already accumulated. Throughout the thirties it continued to be impossible for the western provinces to finance their deficits. In this connection I wish to quote some pages from the Sirois report. On pages 163 and 164 of volume 1, the commission had this to say:
The problem of financing sharply rising outlays for relief would have been difficult enough 
had the costs fallen evenly upon the various sections of the country. The extreme differences which occurred, however, greatly aggravated the situation. The wide disparities and the regional incidence of the depression had, as a consequence, large variations in the incidence of the burden of relief and other welfare costs upon the several provinces.
The costs of relief varied inversely with the ability to meet them. In western Canada, where incomes fell most rapidly, relief costs were relatively the highest. The weight of the burden in Saskatchewan, the province most severely affected, was about five times as great as that in the maritimes and Ontario, the provinces least affected. Total relief expenditures during the eight-year period amounted to nearly two-thirds of the total municipal-provincial revenues in Saskatchewan compared with about one-fifth in the maritimes and Ontario. A burden with such extreme variations in its incidence could not be entirely carried with local resources.
Speaking of the unprecedented problem in the province of Saskatchewan, the commission had this to say at page 170:
The costs of direct and agricultural relief completely overwhelmed the finances of the province and its municipalities. These costs during .1930-37 never fell to less than 27 per cent (1933) of the total municipal-provincial revenues, and in 1937 they rose to 163 per cent of such revenues. For the whole period the relief expenditures amounted to 60 per cent (compared with 21 per cent for the rest of the country) of the total ordinary receipts of the province and its municipalities combined. Although new taxes were imposed and rates increased, revenues could not be maintained at levels required to provide adequate ordinary government services, much less to pay for any part of relief costs. It was manifestly impossible to meet any significant portion of the outlay on relief by means of local taxation when total expenditures for this purpose for the eight-year period exceeded the total net farm cash income of the whole province . . . The provincial government undertook, either directly or indirectly, virtually the whole of the liability in excess of the dominion share. Between 1930 and 1937 the total debt of the provincial government was more than doubled. Three-quarters of this increase was due to relief. In 1929 the per capita deadweight debt of the province of Saskatchewan was the loivest in Canada with the exception of Quebec; in 1937 it was the highest.
Finally, speaking of the western provinces as a whole, the commission said on page 173 of its report:
The western provinces either temporarily or permanently lost their financial independence and could only continue to function with dominion loans and in some cases with partial default of debt charges. In 1937, one-fifth of the total municipal-provincial revenues were absorbed by the interest on non-self-supporting debts.
Of the loans made by the dominion to the four western provinces during this period), an amount aggregating over $165 million is still outstanding, of which Saskatchewan owes $80 million, not counting indebtedness arising out of 1938 seed grain loan guarantees which was

Western Provinces
refunded in 1945 and is now outstanding in the amount of 810,051,707.96; Manitoba nearly S25 million; Alberta S26 million, and British Columbia 834 million.
This indebtedness is secured by treasury bills held by the dominion. The bills all bear three per cent interest, although rates on the earliest loans by the dominion were as high as five per cent. In the case of Saskatchewan, interest has not been paid in recent years on a very substantial proportion of its total indebtedness. The indebtedness is represented by treasury bills which are payable either on demand or at the end of one year. The practice has been to renew the one year treasury bills repeatedly as they came due; and while from time to time small amounts have been paid off by provincial governments, it has been impossible to get any substantial amounts paid off or to put into effect any systematic plan for the retirement of the indebtedness.
As the house will recall, a couple of years ago there was a dispute between the dominion and the province of Saskatchewan in regard to the payment by the province of a demand treasury bill arising out of the guarantee of 1938 seed grain loans in the province. The dominion had endeavoured to use the principle of "offsetting" part of the dominion's payments to the province under the wartime tax agreement against the seed grain loan debt owed by the government of Saskatchewan to the dominion. An arbitration tribunal was set up under the wartime tax agreement to adjudicate upon this dispute but did not reach a unanimous decision. Shortly thereafter a settlement was arranged between the two governments by which the debt was refunded and arrangements made for its repayment over a reasonable period of years.
This controversy served to emphasize the unsatisfactory situation arising out of the indebtedness of these provinces to the dominion and during the negotiations leading to the dominion-ffrovincial agreements it was recognized that as long as there was a possibility of the dominion using the power of "offsetting", no judicial determination of the question having been achieved-

For the purposes of the settlement, the outstanding treasury bills were first divided into two classes, those that represented borrowing for capital or ordinary government purposes, and those that represented borrowing for direct and agricultural relief. It was felt by the dominion that any adjustment granted could relate only to the second category, namely, relief loans.
*Loans for other than, relief purposes, it was felt, should be paid off in full over a reasonable period of years on a systematic amortization basis. It was agreed that the total indebtedness of each province for capital and ordinary government purposes should be refunded by means of a new issue of securities which would be retired over a period of thirty years by equal annual payments representing amortization of principal and interest at 2f per cent, which is approximately the cost of borrowing by the dominion for a comparable period. In order to encourage more rapid repayment if the finance position of a province should make it possible, it is provided that in case a province should pay any amount of principal in advance of the date fixed for payment thereof, interest shall
be deemed to have been payable on the amount so paid at a lesser rate appropriate to the term for which this amount of principal was outstanding. A table will be inserted in each treasury bill showing the interest rates to be used in connection with such prepayments and these rates will correspond approximately to the cost of dominion borrowing for the varying periods in question.
When the legislation has been passed and the arrangement implemented, the new issue of treasury bills which will replace the treasury bills now outstanding issued for capital and ordinary government purposes, will amount in round figures to $13-9 million in the case of Manitoba; $5-4 million in the case of Saskatchewan (after applying the natural resources award payment); $7-6 million in the case of Alberta (after applying the natural resources award payment) and S17-3 million in *the case of British Columbia, a total of just over $44 million.
In the case of the treasury bills which represent provincial borrowing for direct or agricultural relief, the arrangement is that
Western Provinces

half of the bills now outstanding will be cancelled and the other half replaced with a new issue of treasury bills payable, without interest, in equal annual amounts on the first day of July in each of the next thirty years. The total amount of indebtedness which will thus be cancelled is $55,416,164.06, divided as follows: Manitoba, $5,439,675.58; Saskatchewan, $36,336,797.79; Alberta, $5,297,500; and British Columbia, $8,342,190.69.
In the case of Saskatchewan this amount includes $5,726,184.07 of interest on relief treasury bills which was capitalized during the thirities. Prior to 1940-41, Saskatchewan only paid its interest in cash in respect of certain treasury bills issued for capital or ordinary government purposes, and interest on the balance of its treasury bills was paid by the issue of further provincial treasury bills, which, of course, increased the provinces debt to the dominion. No treasury bills in respect of capitalized interest were received after March, 1940, but it should be remembered that under the wartime tax agreements Saskatchewan accepted the net debt service option and consequently had1 the province been paying interest to the dominion on its relief treasury bills, it would have been entitled to receive during the life of the agreement a corresponding increase in the annual amount payable by the dominion under that agreement. This did not seem sensible at the time and no such arrangement was made. I believe the house will agree that the sensible and sound course today; in view of the general settlement which has been reached, is not to continue to carry this capitalized interest dowm through the years but to cancel it as has been arranged.
The. amount of the relief indebtedness which will be refunded by a new issue of treasury bills but without interest aggregates $49,689,980, divided as follows:	Manitoba, $5,439,-
675.58; Saskatchewan, $30,610,613.72; Alberta, $5,297,500,00; and British Columbia, $8,342.190.70.
This completes the description of the essential features of the arrangement. Perhaps I may summarize the position as follows: Today the four western provinces, as a result of their experience in the thirties, owe the dominion some $165 million (excluding the Saskatchewan seed grain loan indebtedness previously referred to). On nearly $74 million of this debt, no interest is currently being paid. Part of the debt is payable on demand and the rest theoretically is payable at the end of one year but in fact it has under present circumstances to be constantly renewed. The debt is carried on the books from year to year with little change and there is no systematic plan for its retirement. When the new agreement is impletMr. Abbott.]
mented, slightly over $16 million of the total debt will be paid1 off in cash and another $55 million will be cancelled. There will then be outstanding almost $94 million of treasury bills, of which slightly over $44 million will bear interest at 2f per cent and the remainder, no interest. Systematic provision, however, will have been made for retiring the whole of this amount in equal annual amounts over a period of thirty years. The annual payments required to be made by each province in order to pay interest and retire the debt should be comfortably within the capacity of the province to pay.
I believe, therefore, that hon. members will agree that this arrangement is one which is in the best interest of the dominion and the provincial governments concerned and will contribute to sounder dominion-provincial financial relationships.

I would like to make a suggestion to the government-that we do not wait until we are faced with a situation under which large sums of money will have to be spent on direct relief.
After all, money expended in that way is not an investment; it is practically wasted, although it is necessary at the time. It would appear to me to be the better part of wisdom if the government would adopt the policy of making available to the western provinces, particularly the three prairie provinces, large sums of money, interest free, probably to the extent of $10,000,000 per year, in order that they may stabilize their economies and open up new fields of industry, such as processing, which industry would fit in so well with the economy of western Canada. That would be making an investment in the western provinces rather than just spending money as a stopgap in the trying times of a depression.
I want to emphasize the fact that this money should be made available interest free, because in reality it will be assisting the people of Canada through the federal government. If we learned a lesson from the last depression it was that if the different governments wait until a depression is upon them and there are thousands of unemployed in need of some direct relief or other form of assistance to keep body and soul together, large sums of money-in the last depression it ran to over a billion dollars-will be spent with practically no return. I hope the government will announce some new policy, perhaps revolutionary for them, of making available to the provinces large sums of money interest free in order that they may prevent the next depression rather than having to spend money when it does come.

Mr. HLYNIvA: When the house took recess at one o'clock I had just concluded putting on the record the three reports which appeared 
in the Daily Tribune stating that one hundred and ten young Canadians were granted permission to attend the youth festival in Prague, Czechoslovakia. I said that the government should have limited this delegation to ten members and reserved the remaining one hundred spaces on ships for British immigrants or displaced persons and refugees to come to Canada. I maintain that an error has been made in granting permission to such a large number of these people to attend the conference, thereby reducing the shipping space, because these people will have to come back to Canada eventually.
One other point in connection with this particular matter has to do with the money which these young people will spend while in Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. The government should have given consideration to that. I do not think we have too much foreign currency to spend as freely as these people no doubt will. I endeavoured to plead the cause of displaced persons and refugees on many occasions, and today I laid emphasis on the advisability of permitting a certain number of displaced persons and refugees who may have education to come in but who are willing to accept farm employment and employment in other lines of endeavour where there is a shortage of labour. The government would do well if it extended its regulations to permit some of these other people to come in. I appeal to thfe minister to give his earnest consideration to that matter.
There are one or two other things that I wish to mention in regard to Ukrainians. It so happens that Roumania was an enemy country during the war and is still looked upon as an enemy country. The Ukrainians who happened to inhabit one province of the Ukrainian historic land, the province of Bucovina, were incorporated into Roumania from the time of the first great war until the second great war, and as residents of Roumania, as they call it, they are considered enemy aliens. They are not I do not think a single Ukrainian who came from Bucovina fought against the British or the allies. The Roumanians held this land, and the Canadian government should be well enough versed in these matters to know that these people were held by force and had nothing to do with the Roumanian army, and for that reason they are not enemy people and should be admitted to Canada. These people should not take the blame for the Roumanian government, because they are neither Roumanians, nor did they ever agree with the occupation of their historic land.
The procedure which the government follows seems to exclude immigrants rather than allow

Supply-Mines and Resources
them to come in. That is the way it appears to me. I did mention that a number of countries, United States, Britain, Brazil, Argentina and a few others, are taking in these people as fast as they can. Until recently it was an urgent question, and of course the government of Canada turned a deaf ear to the pleadings of those who spoke on behalf of displaced persons and refugees. The government rendered lip service, issued statements and passed regulations, but in effect did very little to allow these people to come in. It is now a matter of being fortunate if we get a number of these people, because when the United States, Britain and other countries that are taking these people get through there will be nothing left for us. Surely we should realize that in the future we shall not be able to get any European people to come to Canada, at least from countries that are today held or dominated by the Soviet union. Therefore why not take them now; why not take the best possible element? I would urge the government to give earnest consideration to that recommendation.
In this connection I should like to mention that I have in my hand a number of letters, and I shall read one or two sentences from one of them. They are from displaced persons who were fortunate enough to be accepted by Belgium. Here is one:
I am very son-y that you did not come with us to work at the Belgian mines.
He is writing to one of his friends.
The people are working hard here, but they are earning money and are able to buy everything they like. You can buy everything in Belgium if you have francs except the bird's milk. The shops are full of wares. After my life in Germany I cannot believe that it is really so. It seems that I am dreaming, that I am in America. It is really America in Europe. All information we read in newspapers were true. I am glad that I left Germany and the UNRRA's care. Although I have no money in my pocket, I feel that I am in a proper place here. The food is very good. We now get 4,000 calories per day.
The Belgians are showing a good attitude towards us. I advise you to come to Belgium as soon as possible. If you can't do it, tell other people to go to Belgium.
I regret that we do not receive such letters from newcomers to Canada telling their friends that Canada, recognizing the contribution of those who have come to this country as immigrants, is giving present-day immigrants an opportunity to make a living and opening up to them the possibility of a future. I could read many more of these letters, but I do not think I should at this time.
I wish to refer to only one other matter which I do not think I have mentioned before.
It is in connection with families who were separated throughout the war and are separated even today. I have here a list of names of people in the various zones, British, American and French, in Germany, Austria and Italy, where the husband is in one country and the wife with a child in another, and so far they have been unable to get together. I also have several replies from camp and zone directors stating, "We are sorry, but you cannot join your husband", or "You cannot join your wife and kiddies". Although this may not be directly connected with the department of immigration, I would ask that this government recommend to the governments which have a say in these matters that these people be allowed to get together. I realize that this country does not play a large part in international affairs. Though our country is large in area, our population is so small that we are not in the category of a large nation-though the hon. member for Temiscouata usually feels that Canada is being slighted if anyone refers to this country as a secondary or smaller nation; he does not like that. But in reality, in international affairs, we must admit that she is. I do not expect this government to right all these injustices in the international field. I realize that Canada cannot do that. But Canada can make recommendations, and Canada can help these people by allowing a certain number of them to come in. Once again I ask that this be done. I may be quite critical at times, but if better results than we have had thus far are not forthcoming, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that not only myself but all others who are interested in this subject, from the point of view of Canada and from the humanitarian point of view, will really have to get at the government and create public opinion to make the government move in the direction in which they should.
