I feel that the hon. member for Vegreville has made some strong statements, many of which are quite erroneous. I think his statements should not be allowed to stand without the correct facts being put on Hansard. With your indulgence, sir, I should like to reply to the remarks he has just made.
The hon. member has repeated the cry that the government has no immigration policy. Apparently he has not followed the statements made in this house by the minister of the department and the statements that have been made in recent debate, even as late as last evening. The fact is that the government has a specific, well-rounded and coordinated policy of immigration. It is being applied actively and energetically by an expanded and competent branch of the department. The policy may be described briefly as follows:
1.	There is practically free entry for all citizens of the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Ireland.
2.	There is equally free entry for all citizens of the United States.
3.	Citizens of non-enemy European countries may enter Canada if destined to relatives here who are in a position to assist them to get started, or if they are coming to work in agriculture, mining, lumbering or other basic industries.
4.	Other persons from such countries who have adequate means are also admitted freely.
5.	Individuals in the displaced persons camps are admitted to Canada when applied for by close relatives in this country. This is outside the special quota of 10,000 which was authorized as to 5,000 on June 6, 1947, and as to a further 5,000 on July 9 last.
6.	A person applying for admission to Canada for the purpose of marrying a legal resident of this country is admitted if the prospective husband is in a position to maintain his intended wife.
7.	In order to carry this policy into effective operation, we have established offices which can handle immigration cases, not only in the United Kingdom and the United States, but also in Paris, The Hague, Brussels, Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Greece, Czechoslovakia, Portugal, Poland, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Ireland, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, China, Argentina,
[The Deputy Chairman.]
Brazil, Chile, Peru, Cuba, Mexico, Switzerland and India. In addition, we have special teams operating in Germany in cooperation with the preparatory committee of the international refugee organization, to handle the movement of persons from the displaced persons camps.
8.	From time to time movements such as that of the 4,500 members of the Polish armed forces who were recently admitted are approved and their admission to this country facilitated.
9.	Except for the wives and minor families of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin and similar relatives of Canadian citizens or residents of East Indian origin, there is at present no provision for oriental immigration to Canada.

I
should like to be clear in my own mind as to what the minister said. I thought he said any relative of a Canadian citizen resident in a non-enemy country of Europe could come to Canada. Would this mean that the cousin of a Canadian, resident with his wife in Poland, would be entitled to come to Canada?
No; a cousin is not within the published list of relatives. They include a son, daughter, wife or orphan nephew or niece, et cetera, but not cousins.
I ask that question because outside this house a certain misinterpretation is placed upon the word "relative"; that is why I am glad to have the matter clarified.

I might also point out to my hon. friend that the word "cousin" is an almost all-inclusive term if we go back far enough. On May 1, 1947, order in council P.C. 1734, further amended by P.C. 695, made provision for the admission of the husband or wife, son, daughter, brother or sister, together with husband or wife and unmarried children, if any, and orphan nephew or niece under twenty-one years of age of any person legally resident in Canada in a position to' receive and care for such relatives. The new order also provided for the admission of a person enter. ing Canada for the purpose of marriage to a legal resident thereof, provided the prospective husband is able to maintain his intended wife.
The situation with respect to the admission of persons from the displaced persons camps has been explained repeatedly in this house and outside. On June 9 I said in the house, at page 3916 of Hansard:
The 5,000 individuals to be covered by this order will include those displaced persons who have already been admitted. They need not be residents of Canada.

In spite of these facts the hon. member for Vegreville apparently is still unacquainted with the situation. In his speech this morning he gave it as his understanding that only certain persons could be brought into Canada from displaced persons camps, and went on to read the list of persons who are admissible generally from any non-enemy European country. We have 'been admitting relatives within the defined categories from the displaced persons camps for many months. On June 6 it was announced in this house that we wmuld admit 5,000 persons from these camps without waiting for an international agreement on the subject. Last evening I stated that the government had agreed to admit a further 5,000. This total of 10,000 persons does not include relatives but is additional to them. For the most part the movement consists of large groups coming to industrial or other employment in Canada. In addition to that, however, we are admitting individuals and families who are, not applied for by relatives in Canada but who are applied for by other persons in this country who agree to assist in their settlement.
At one point in his statement the hon. member suggested that the Canadian immigration authorities were discriminating against Likrainians. Of course there is not the slightest element of truth in this suggestion. The immigration regulations are not weighted against the Ukrainians, and in the administration of those regulations people of all national groups are treated precisely the same. If I understood him aright the hon. member for Vegreville seemed to suggest that this government was in some way responsible for the repatriation of a large number of Ukrainians from the displaced persons camps in the British and American zones. He indicated that a large number of these people were repatriated against their will. The regulations in regard to Repatriation, as my hon. friend must know, were agreed to by all the occupying forces; and included in them was a provision that no one should be repatriated against his will unless he had been a collaborator with the enemy during the war. For my part I am satisfied that this regulation has been carried out in good faith by the British and American authorities in Germany.
There is another point in the hon. member's statement which I am not prepared to allow to pass unanswered. I refer to his wholly unjustified reference to Mr. Fiorello LaGuardia, at one time mayor of New York city and1 later director general of UNKRA. Mr. LaGuardia is a great friend of Canada and a personal friend of mine, and as chairman of the United States section of the permanent joint board on defence, and in many other ways, he has shown his friendship and respect for this country. He is, moreover, one of those who has worked most ardently on behalf of the displaced persons of Europe.
I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to whom the hon. member for Vegreville referred in eulogistic terms and who knows the situation of European refugees as well as anyone in this country, would fully substantiate my statement. To suggest that Mayor LaGuardia is a communist or a friend of communists is palpably absurd.
Then my hon. friend made the statement two or three times that the United States is taking displaced persons "as fast as it can." I should like to ask him when those persons were taken into the United States, and on what authority. To the best of my knowledge and belief not a single displaced person has been accepted in the United States to date, outside the quota.

I should like to correct one or two statements made by the minister, which I feel were quite unfair. I do not blame him for the government's immigration policy, for he is only pinch-bitting for another minister who happens to be ill at the present time. I feel that results speak loudest. I have in my office several hundred cases of Canadians applying for the admission to Canada of both close and distant relatives, and that permission has not been obtained from the immigration branch. If the minister wishes to assure me that no obstacle will be placed in the way of granting permission in these cases I will be the first to give him and the government credit for that step. I have no reason at all to endeavour to discredit the government or reflect upon its policy. All I want to do is see that this thing gets moving, because so far the results have not been very substantial. The minister said I seemed to suggest that the Canadian government was responsible in some way for the repatriation of many of these displaced persons, and he went on to say he had full confidence that the British and American governments would adhere to their word once they promised not to repatriate any of these people by force. One must study the situation closely to learn the truth. I must tell the minister that it depends largely on the type of man who is in charge of a camp as to whether or not the people are repatriated. Let me say at once that at least fifty per cent of the camp directors working under UNRRA and the military governments have been exceptionally good to these people. Some of them really went out of their way to help; they were humanitarians. About twenty-five per cent

were more or less indifferent; they carried out their instructions and 'that is about all. But I would say that the remaining twenty-five per cent of the heads of UNRRA camps had no business in any humanitarian organization. I was there; I met them; I discussed these problems with them, and their attitude was almost that of persons serving a country in whose interest it was to destroy these people or at least make them as miserable as possible. I have received hundreds of letters andl I have seen -these conditions myself. If the minister states that I am unfair in the assertion that these people are being repatriated, I wish to put on record an UNRRA order, UNRRA U.S. zone headquarters, Heidelberg, November 11, 1946. It is as follows:
Soviet proclamations, literature, films and newspapers will be distributed.
That is, in the camps.
Some such material is now available for distribution and additional material has been promised by Soviet officials. Cultural activities will be utilized and turned -toward the theme of repatriation . . . Every advantage must be taken to utilize the sentiments of persons who accept repatriation. This will call for alertness on the part of repatriation officers and area directors. As the programme gains momentum the experience of mass appeal already gained in the Polish repatriation drive can be brought to fruition with these nationalities. The propitious time for the use of emotional devices will be left to the judgment of the district officers and area teams. Special status with UNRRA will be accorded repatriates in all camp affairs and priorities for basic needs will be arranged on existing stocks of clothing and amenity supplies. Lists of Soviet citizens who lived in the USSR prior to the list -September, 1939, and determined to be Soviet citizens by the military authorities-
That is the screening or army review board.
-and receiving UNRRA care will be forwarded to UNRRA district headquarters by the 1st of December, 1946, where they will be consolidated and then transmitted to U,S. zone headquarters who m turn can transmit them to G.5 third U.S. army for ultimate transmission to the Soviet liaison mission.
_ That is plain enough. Many of these people in camps have been kidnapped. It so happens that an unscrupulous head of a camp will leave the camp for the evening and that evening the Soviet liaison officers will come in and call out certain names and ask these people to appear, and1 when they appear that is the last time they are seen or heard of.
I am not blaming the Canadian government at all for this but- I am pointing to the urgency of the situation as applied to people who lived within the territory held by the Soviet union on September 1, 1939. That is [Mr. Hlynka.J
the only reason I brought the matter up. The minister also said that I was unfair in my suggestion that the government discriminated against Ukrainians, but we have the figures tabled by the director of immigration, Mr. Jolliffe, in the immigration and labour committee, given in the report I quoted. I wish to be fair. As the Minister of Labour pointed out, there were a few others, just a few, who came in as Poles and perhaps under other nationalities, the reason being that some of these people are compelled to change their nationality, to say they are Poles or something else, because otherwise they would be repatriated.
To Russia.

Yes, to Russia, under force; and we in Canada are engaged in this house many hours a day discussing human rights and fundamental freedoms and all the rest of it. Surely if we are sincere in that regard this is one place where we could make our representations. I know the Canadian government has made representations.
As regards my remarks with reference to the former Mayor LaGuardia, the minister says that he is one of Canada's friends, but it does not mean that he is a friend of displaced persons simply because he is Canada's friend. Item 577 reads:

I understand the ruling is that I can speak under this item. I would have been finished with this matter long ago if I had been allowed to speak. I do not intend to take up very much time. I was disappointed with the statement made yesterday by the minister that subsidies were being paid only to the Dominion Coal Company. At that time the minister said that he got his authority from the report of the royal commission on coal. I have gone through that report very carefully and I find that that commission recommended subventions and
Supply-Mines and Resources

tariffs as a means of assisting coal mining in the maritime provinces. On page 584 of the report is a supplementary note which looks to me more like an after thought than anything else. It is signed by W. F. Carroll, the chairman of the committee and it reads:
I think that it may be necessary to afford the Cape Breton mines interim support immediately following the suspension of production subsidies arising out of price control.
That apparently is the basis for the payment of subsidies to the Dominion Coal Company in Nova Scotia. The Dominion Coal Company is the largest producer in the mari-times, and if it needs assistance, surely the smaller producers-I speak particularly for those in New Brunswick-need similar assistance. The Dominion Coal Company has received more assistance than any of the smaller companies. Not only do we not have a subsidy in New Brunswick; we are faced with the fact that the Dominion Coal Company has received more assistance than any of the smaller companies. Not only do we not have a subsidy in New Brunswick; we are faced with the fact that the Dominion Coal Company is paid a subvention to ship coal into New Brunswick to compete with the small mines there.
I do not wish to give offence to the minister, but I do contend that if this policy is continued it will drive this small industry in New Brunswick out of business. I do not want to be insistent, but I must emphasize that this industry means much to the people down there. To a great extent our whole economy depends upon our coal mines. Our hydro electric power is developed from our coal which is sold almost exclusively in our own province. If the government is going to continue to pay subventions to the coal industry in Nova Scotia to ship coal into New Brunswick to compete against the smaller mines there, it will drive those people out of business.
I had a letter just a day or so ago protesting against this and calling attention to the report that the president of the Dominion Coal Company had said that they were negotiating for subsidies. I feel keenly about this matter and that is why I have brought it to the attention of the minister again. I have great confidence in the minister and I submit that this is a matter which should receive his personal attention.
I think the cost of the royal commission on coal was out of all proportion to the benefits the coal industry has derived from its investigations. I was just looking up the cost of producing this large book and carrying

on the investigations and I find it was $282,374. As far as I can find out the only recommendations that have been carried out have been to appoint a dominion coal board, which could have been set up without any investigation of this kind, and carrying out the recomendation in a footnote by one of the members of the commission, Mr. Justice Carroll, a footnote which is not signed by the other members. That recommendation is simply to help the Dominion Coal Company. I make no apology for bringing up this matter at this time, and I sincerely hope the minister will give it the consideration it deserves.

It seems to me that the question of immigration falls roughly under three headings. First, there is the desire of the Canadian people to assist and relieve suffering in foreign countries. Second, there is the uniting of families. Third, there is the building up of our own country in a strong and efficient way. There has been a certain fictional romanticism about the efforts of the premier of Ontario to bring a certain number of immigrants to this country.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear applause from certain quarters and I hope the hon. members approve of it. In order to expedite matters I wonder if the Acting Minister of Mines and Resources would state whether any arrangements have been made by the British government for the settlement of immigrants in Canada.

I know of no arrangements made by the British government. British immigrants are received freely here and the services of the department of immigration and the Department of Labour are devoted to placing them properly in employment. That is the only arrangement that I know of.

Certain publicity has been given to the statement by the premier of Ontario that the British government have made certain arrangements for the settlement of immigrants in Canada. The minister says that there is nothing of that sort?
Do you mean the Ontario government?
The Ontario government has had a certain amount of publicity by stating that the British government have made plans for the settling of people in different commonwealth countries.

I have the literature published under the seal of the agent general of Ontario,

Supply-Mines and Resources
issued from Ontario House, 13 Charles II street, London, and the plan as given in this literature says:
The Ontario government has contracted by charter with the Transoeean Airlines Company of California, to supply daily two Skymasters each carrying 40 passengers to fly from Britain during August, September and October. The immigrants pay the full passage fare and are transported at Toronto, Ontario. The proposition is merely one of offering increased facilities to permit emigrants to move. There is no other intention or obligation on the part of the Ontario government.
Upon arrival the immigrant is interviewed and offered certain employment opportunities based on his capabilities; also living accommodation suggested. He is under no compulsion to accept what is offered. If he has some prearranged employment, he need not use the facilities of the placement officer, and he is at liberty to seek his own job.	_
No guarantees are given by^ the Ontario government of employment or living accommodation, hut the immigrant may be assured that many opportunities exist and that every reasonable assistance will be given if he wishes to avail himself of the service.	*
Another paragraph reads:
Only the following need apply.
Ages:	Male-16 to 17J-with parents' consent.
Ex-military service up to 21-with parents' consent. 21 to 40 inclusive.
Female-21 to 45 inclusive.
The Ontario government has asked for the cooperation of the federal government, and the full cooperation of the immigration department has been offered. The great difficulty of the plan is that the Ontario government has made what purports to be a contract with a United States air carrier with a business based on California. But Canada has a reciprocal agreement with the United Kingdom which provides that only Canadian or British equipment may fly the United Kingdom-Canada Atlantic route, and which provides further for a division of the traffic on that route between the United Kingdom and Canada. Canada is also a signatory of the international air transport agreement, which provides that certain rates will apply for certain periods on the Atlantic. This Ontario plan cuts across both these agreements. There is no possible way in which a United States carrier could carry traffic between the United Kingdom and Canada under existing international arrangements. Canada must take the view that it must keep its agreement with the United Kingdom and therefore it cannot permit a United States plane operating between the United Kingdom and Canada to land in Canada.
I believe that the proposal now is to land in the United States and transport the passengers
thence to Canada by buses. That will protect Canada so far as our agreement goes. It does not protect the United Kingdom, and it leaves the United States in rather a peculiar position. However, Canada is satisfied to protect our own good faith in carrying out our agreement, and we shall be happy if the movement can proceed without involving any violation on our part. It seems reasonable to expect that, if a province wishes to engage in a charter air operation, it should apply to either a British or Canadian aviation company for the necessary equipment. Charter equipment is freely available in England and in Canada. This seems to be a perfect example of a man playing with machinery that he did not understand and getting his fingers cut. However, no movement by air has :taken place as yet under the Ontario plan.
Who pays the cost of these immigrants flying to this country?

As I understand it, the
Ontario government has guaranteed full loads, and in consideration of that guarantee the fare is reduced by about S50 or $60 below the normal Atlantic crossing rate. The Ontario government has in effect relieved the carrier of all the cost of booking passengers, and of all the loss that occurs through passengers not appearing at the time of the departure of the plane. From the point of view of the aircraft operator the charter is attractive, but from the point of view of competition with other carriers it places the United States company in a preferred position. Although it purports to be a charter, it is my understanding that tickets for this service are being sold through a travel agency in London.
What percentage of the immigrants coming to Canada in 1946 and in 1947 to date were from the British isles, and what percentage from continental European countries?

For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, the totals of English, Irish, Scottish and Welsh were 20,162; from the United States, 7,454; northern European races, 1,148; all other races, 2,317, or a grand total of 31,081, of which more than 20,000 came from the British isles.
Has the minister the figures up to March 31, 1947?

For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947, 47,976 were from the United Kingdom, 11,410 from the United States, 5.605 from northern European races, and
Supply-Mines and Resources

1,999 from other races, so that over 47,000 out of a total of almost 67,000 were from the United Kingdom.
Are the wives and children of service men included in those figures?
I understand that these figures are for all immigrants, and show that more than two-thirds of our immigration came from the United Kingdom.
Then when the premier of Ontario says that most of the immigrants coming to Canada are foreigners-
He would not say anything like that. You are playing politics.
He said foreigners and other European nationals. I take it from the figures given by the minister that the statement of the premier of Ontario is not correct.

It is not correct. I can read the statement in the Ontario literature:
Many continentals and foreigners are now being permitted to enter Canada. We feel it essential that we maintain our present percentages of British stock.
The 4,000 Poles who were brought in cannot be included in the last figures the minister gave. The number amounted to 4,000. When did they come in?
That movement occurred after March 31, 1947.
Some more of these are being brought in.
No.
I am told some were brought in before and some after. Those who came in before March 31 would be included in the figure I gave; those who came after would not.

The management of pounds sterling is, of course, a matter for the Bank of England and for the Chancellor of the Exchequer of Great Britain. The practice has been that immigrants with small means are allowed a greater proportion of their means in the first year than people better off. I think that any man desiring to emigrate to Canada is given sufficient money to satisfy Canadian regulations that he shall have funds sufficient to take care of him until he becomes established, which is a very small amount. I might point out that it would be difficult for Canada to get excited about this situation, because Canadians who wished to emigrate to another country have not been allowed to take all their funds; they have been allowed to take only a limited amount.

In going over the definite policies of the government a few moments ago the minister said something that I did not quite understand. There are two people from Lebanon in Syria who applied to come to Canada, a mother and a son eighteen years of age. I want to know whether I understood the minister aright, that these people could not come here now. There are also two Polish residents, a man and his wife. They have relatives in Canada who are anxious to bring these two people here. There is also a family from Holland, quite a wealthy man, who wants to go into business in this country. Did I understand correctly that these five people whom I have mentioned could, under the new regulations, come to Canada? Their relatives are here.

I made it very clear in my statement that except for certain classes, which I have mentioned, there is no provision in the Canadian Immigration Act for Asiatics. Lebanon is in Asia. That situation is being studied and there may be a change in the regulations; but at the present time the people of Lebanon are not admissible under the Canadian regulations. What is the occupation of these Polish people? Where are they?

The man and his wife want to come out here to farm. Their people are already in Canada. They have two brothers living in Montreal and two brothers living in Charlottetown. They are splendid people, good citizens. They are in a position to establish themselves. Their people here are willing to put up bonds that they will not become a burden on the state.
They are admissible if they are in good health.

The minister said, as I understood him-perhaps I misunderstood him -that the Canadian government could not get excited about this since the same condition applied to Canadians leaving Canada, that they were not allowed to take all their assets. Did I understand the minister to say that?
Yes.

How was it that the group of Slavs who left Canada recently were allowed to take their assets with them? They were Canadian citizens. They took their assets. Surely we should have some arrangement whereby British emigrants coming to this country could bring their assets in.
Mr. HQW'E: The people to whom my hon. friend referred were allowed to take certain assets out. Of some of them who had a considerable fortune in Canada, they were not allowed to take all their fortunes.
It depends on exchange.
No, it does not depend on exchange.
There is lots of sterling.
There may be lots of sterling, but my hon. friend may get all the sterling he wants to spend in England.

May I ask the minister a question with regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Melfort. Have there been any discussions between the Department of Finance and the Department of Mines and Resources, immigration branch, in regard to putting Canadian dollars at the disposal of the United Kingdom authorities to assist immigrants from Great Britain who have some capital there which they wish to transplant into this country, so that there will be a source of Canadian funds which can be drawn upon in exchange for sterling balances? I ask this question apart from the general financial considerations which exist between Great Britain and Canada in regard to Canadian dollars. What I want to know is, has the * Department of Immigration had any conversations with the United Kingdom to obviate the difficulty which the hon. member mentioned?
Not to my knowledge.

May I also ask the minister a question in regard to the transportation by air which was arranged by the premier of Ontario. The minister said that the T.C.A. or some transport service in Canada operated by T.C.A. had equipment which could do this particular job; also that the contract was a very desirable one. On that premise may I ask the minister whether or not T.C.A. ever approached the premier of Ontario with the suggestion that their services would be at the disposal of the province of Ontario to assist in the transportation of British immigrants?
Trans-Canada Air Lines have indeed approached the Ontario government.
Did they approach the Ontario government before the contract was made with the United States company?
Unfortunately Trans-Canada Air Lines did not happen to be in England at the proper time. The contract was, I understand, made in England.
Did I understand the minister to say that Premier Drew was out of line when he arranged for the flying of immigrants here from the old country?

No, I do not say that at all. I said he was out of line when he arranged for an American plane to fly between Canada and the United Kingdom.

To follow up again the
question I asked before, in a letter from the foreign exchange control board with regard to this matter, it is stated:
Since the loans would be made against sterling assets not yet eligible for transfer to Canada, the foreign exchange control board does not have authority to use its assets for such purposes-
And this is the part I wish to bring to the minister's attention.
-and the question becomes one of general government policy.
In my humble opinion the government should have a policy with regard to this, to assist in the matter of British immigrants transferring their assets over here. I just wanted to state our position in that matter, because I think it is important that these people, especially those having assets of two or three thousand pounds or under, should nave such assets made available to them on their arrival in Canada so that they can oecome established. Otherwise they simply cannot purchase a home at all and become established. Their assets are dissipated over a period of three or four years and very often to little purpose.

I just wish to refer
to a few of the remarks made by the hon. member for Yegreville who, I think, was most unfair in charging the government with discrimination as far as his people are concerned. I say that because I think the hon. member seems to permit himself to be misinformed. To support my contention, I want to read from a Canadian press dispatch of April 2, 1946, as follows:
On March 25, Anthony Hlynka, Social Credit member of the Canadian House of Commons for Vegreville, Alta., said he had been informed in a letter from reliable British and Canadian sources overseas that a group of drunken Cana-
dian occupation troops were led by a Russian officer into Wesserflug displaced persons camp at Delmenhorst, Germany, February 1 and February 2. There, according to the letter, they seized ninety Ukrainians and took them into the Russian zone.
The reply to that, in the Canadian press dispatch from London, of the officials concerned, reads as follows:
Canadian troops in northwest Germany have been participating in a search of displaced person camps for Russian citizens who must be repatriated to the Russian zone under military government regulations, Canadian military headquarters here said yesterday.
Opposition to deportation has been encountered from some displaced persons, officials said, particularly those Russian citizens who have "guilty consciences" because of cooperation with the Germans during the war. In some instances force has been required to send the "D.P's" to the Russian zone.
Persons suspected of being Russians are removed from displaced persons camps and appear before special board which determines their nationality. Any Russians are then sent to the Russian zone under military government policy.
In addition to that, these reports were brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence, who asked for a report from the commander overseas at that time. I am quite sure that if the report on this matter of the commander of the Canadian forces in Germany at that time was read to this committee, hon. members would fully appreciate the kind of people they were dealing with in this instance.

Under item 185 I wish to take a little time to refer to the question of immigration. On the general policy of immigration I believe it is not necessary to say much more. We have discussed it in this house before. I have been trying to find some disinterested authority which might give some clue as to what effect a policy of greater immigration may have upon our country, and this may be of general interest to the committee. I have come across the reprint of an article written by R. H. Coats, the retired dominion statistician, which appeared in Saturday Night. Quoting from his article, they have this to say, which I think gives us some lead as to what we may expect:
Statistical records show that periods of high immigration are also periods of rising wage levels, says the retired dominion statistician, who is one of the world's chief authorities on the subject and is now a special lecturer at the university of Toronto.
Then a direct quotation from Mr. Coats:
The trend of wages, like that of prices and the cost of living, is contingent primarily upon the condition of the economy as a whole, and will not suffer from immigration if the latter is economically sound.
I think that sets out in brief terms the proper approach to the question of general immigration; that is to say, that if our economy is properly planned in such a way that we may expand the economy together with an expanding population, there is then no danger of unemployment or a dropping of wage scales.
I will leave that part of it at that point and go on with the other question which has been discussed today and which I believe the committee is more interested in at this time. That is the question of the displaced persons, the refugees, to which reference has been made by several hon. members today. On other occasions I have been critical of the government in connection with this matter, but today I want to quote from a document which gives the government a certain amount of credit, because I believe we should give credit where it is due. This is a memorandum submitted to the government by the Ukrainian Canadian committee in March of this year, and the paragraph I wish to quote I believe is very fair. It reads:
With regard to the second problem, namely the settlement of refugees, we wish to express our sincere thanks to the Canadian government
Supply-Mines and Resources

for its action and tlie humanitarian stand taken by its delegation at the recent conference of the united nations. We have also noted with deep gratitude the fact that our country, Canada, was the first of all nations to sign the charter of the international refugee organization, which was created at the united nations conference. We believe that the Canadian government will continue its present course towards the final solution of the refugee problem. It is our belief that the government of Canada will serve as an example to governments of other countries in the resettlement of refugees and displaced persons by opening its doors more generously.
That is a bouquet thrown to the government, which I hope will not have the effect of making them rest on their laurels. I hope they will continue to take vigorous action in this matter in order that these people, whom we have referred to so often in this house and who are suffering in the displaced persons camps of Europe, may be relieved of their misery as quickly as may be humanly possible.
In that connection I want to add that when we last discussed this question in this house I offered a recommendation to the government. To what extent it has been carried out, I am not in a position to say. I recommended then that the most careful consideration should be given to allowing to come to Canada from the displaced persons camps persons who have relatives in Canada in a position to look after them and give them a start in life. I know there are thousands of applications in the immigration office. I know many members of this house have in their own files hundreds of letters regarding these applications for permission to bring relatives to Canada. Unfortunately the rate at which these applications have been handled and the rate at which permission is being granted is disappointing. We do not oppose the entry of other people to Canada.	I
believe the action of the government in passing only yesterday, an order in council under which an additional five thousand will be permitted to enter Canada will meet with approval across the country. But there is general disappointment at the speed with which these applications are being handled. There is a special urgency, because many of these people applied months ago. Some of these applications have been before the officials for two years now. If action is to be taken this year it can easily be seen that it must be done immediately. We are now in the month of July, and it is not long until the harvest season. If people are to become established here it is much better to let them come in now, when they can be of some assistance to their relatives in Canada and at the same time have a few months of the summer season left in which to become estab-

l'ished. That would be far better than having them come in the late fall or winter months. Therefore I hope some special effort will be made to expedite the handling of these applications, so that people waiting for permission to enter the country may have something to which they can look forward.
I also mentioned to the government the advisability of giving those who are now in displaced persons camps, and on whose behalf applications have been made, some statement to this effect in documentary form. Many of those people do not regularly receive information from Canada; in fact most of them do not. In some cases newspapers are not available, and for most of those people it is difficult to correspond with their relatives in Canada. They do not even know whether application has been made on their behalf. It places them in an uncertain position, and that uncertainty and suspense in their own minds is very bad for their morale. I would suggest-and I do not think it would involve very much extra expense or work-that when an application is received by the department from a person in Canada on behalf of a relative in a displaced persons camp, the person on whose behalf that application has been made be notified of that fact immediately and be given some document to indicate that fact. Then he will know that as soon as he becomes eligible, as soon as transportation is available, if he meets the qualifications of the immigration department he- will be able to proceed to Canada. He will have a document to show the officials of the camp and any other authorities concerned, and will have the satisfaction of knowing that some action is being taken on his behalf. It would also have the effect of giving those people something to look forward to in the future. As we all know, the relief that has been given so generously to those people by UNRRA is now being terminated. Many of them will have to leave the displaced persons camps, perhaps not of their own choice, but through the necessity of earning a living. It is not going to be easy for them to decide whether to establish a home somewhere in the country in which they happen to be or still to plan on coming to Canada, unless they have something in their possession to show that someone in Canada is working on their behalf to bring them here.
I wish also to ask the minister to comment on the position of people who are now classified as enemy aliens; that is, people who, during the war, happened to be in countries which were fighting against the allies. Many of those people are not really nationals of those countries. They happened to be there by reason of geography, or because of changes

Supply-Mines and Resources
in geography over which they had no control. The example of Roumania was brought up today, and there are other cases of people of a different nationality who happened to be in those countries when war was declared and who are now regarded as enemy aliens until the peace treaties are ratified. I would ask the minister to comment on what position they will be in once the peace treaties are ratified, whether they will be treated like all other people in European countries; also what possibility there is of such people being able to prove that they are not truly nationals of the country under whose jurisdiction they came without consent and often against their own will. Many of those people were strongly opposed to the nazi regimes of those countries; some were actively opposed in the way of resistance movements, while others were perhaps just passively opposed. We could hardly expect women and children to be actively opposed to those governments. However, they are now in the position that, owing to an accident of geography, they are classified as enemy aliens. They may have very close relatives in Canada; we have cases where a father in Canada wants to bring his son or daughter from a European country, but because that son or daughter happened to be in a country like Roumania or another country in a similar position, they are classified as enemy aliens and at the present time are not eligible for entry. I hope the minister will make some statement on that position.
The other question I should like to ask is in connection with Poland. Some time ago I inquired of the department as to whether any information was available concerning the position being taken by Poland with regard to people who wished to leave that country and come to Canada. On March 7 of this year I received from the director of the immigration branch a reply in which he said in part:
We are not yet in a position to state whether or not the Polish government permits emigration from that country. The position at the moment is that we have no facilities for the examination of immigrants in the country named. However, there will be Canadian representation in Poland very shortly and we then hope to be able to arrange for immigration inspectional facilities if immigrants can leave that country.
I am wondiering whether any change has taken place since March of this year, whether any representations have been made since that time, and what attitude, if any, has been taken by the Polish government on this question.	.
There is only one more question I wish to raise, and that is along the lines of a question raised! by an hon. member to my right today. In connection wdth people who are 83166-348
known in Canada as Armenians, I have received documents and letters from certain persons interested in this matter who have asked me to raise this question in the house in order to get some clarification as to where Armenians stand under the immigration regulations. According to the regulations at the present time, Asiatic races are excluded, and apparently under order in council P.C. 2115 Armenians are regarded as Asiatics. I have the following information from a gentleman interested in the matter. He tells me that Mr. C. E. S. Smith, an official of the department wrote to him on May 10, 1947, a letter in which he stated:
With respect to your comment regarding Armenian nationals I would inform you that order in council P.C. 2115 covering such matters is based on geographic and not ethnological grounds. In view of the location of Armenia nationals of that country come within the scope of the order in council mentioned.
In other words, the interpretation of the regulations is such that people coming from what is known as Armenia are considered ito be Asiatics. I have documentary evidence signed by two professors of the university of Montreal, both professors of history in that institution, who apparently have made an exhaustive study of the question. They inform me that the Armenians are of Indo-European culture, race, language and civilization. They are of Aryan origin. Geographically speaking, they state, Armenia is situated in Trans-Caucausia, which is generally included in Europe. They say, further, that many Armenians were born in Constantinople, a European city which is situated on the European continent.
I have no reason to question the information given me by these gentlemen, who, as I say, have made a study of the question. I merely raise the matter, so that the officials of the department may make a closer study of the situation and clarify the regulations in order to be able to prove in their own minds whether the Armenians are actually an Asiatic race. From information given me, and from the studies I have made on the subject, it appears to me that they may more properly be classified as European than as an Asiatic race. These are simply a few points I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and I would ask him to comment upon them.

I should like to say a word or two about immigration and give one illustration. A man in Toronto has a brother in Poland who is eligible to come to Canada. The man in Poland has a son who is eligible to come to Canada. But his daughter-in-law is not eligible. It seems to me that that kind of thing ought to be straightened out. We should not be dividing families. I do not see any reason why a family should be broken up, especially when they are fine people. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Spadina. There are many good people in Europe who would like to come to Canada and who would be an asset to this country. We need population; we need the right kind of people. The immigration branch is doing a big work right at the present time. I come back to the theme that is worrying me and ask that the immigration branch facilitate the movement of these executives of industry into this country. I have in mind a man by the name of H. W. Orwell who recently arrived in Canada. This man is full of know-how from British scientific manufacturing institutions. He is here on only a year's permit. He is a [DOT]S10.000 a year man, highly schooled and technically trained, to a degree which no one else in Canada has attained. He finds himself here, but his daughter was left behind. My plea in a few sentences is this. Take a broad view of those who want to come to

live among us, those who are trained, those who are executives, those who will expand industry, those who will be a great credit to this country, those who are enthusiastic over the idea that Canada has a future, that perhaps in days to come Canada will be the centre of gravity as far as the empire is concerned. Let us in Canada see if we cannot at this time capture these world markets which, before the war, were served by Europe, Germany and Belgium in particular, and, to a lesser degree, by Italy and perhaps Holland. With all these people anxious to come to our shores to help us develop our natural resources, let us see if we are not big enough in this assembly to take full advantage of the situation by admitting these people to our shores instead of holding them back by picayune regulations. Let us admit these people of good will who want to come here and who can give Canada the know how that has been accumulated over the generations in Britain and in Europe.

I say once again, as I have said three or four times this afternoon and once last evening, that any resident of British race in Great Britain who is of good character and in good health and has a small sum of money sufficient to maintain him until he can establish himself here is entitled to come to Canada, and not the slightest obstacle will be put in his way.

It is clear enough, but it breaks up the family. A man can bring in his son, but he cannot bring in his daughter-in-law. I have one such case that I have been trying to do something about. But when a man comes here and becomes a resident of Canada he can immediately apply to have his son and daughter brought in. It seems an anomalous thing.
My hon. friend will have to go to work on the regulations. We cannot extend them this afternoon.
I am going to see that the regulations are broadened. The present regulations break up families.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a problem that I believe Canada should attend to now. For a long time we have as a nation been dreaming of the time when we should have a trans-Canada highway. I believe the time

Supply-Mines and Resources
has come to build such a highway, so that it will not be necessary for Canadians to submit to the indignity of going into a foreign country to get from their capital to their own coast. A great deal of interest has been generated recently in the four western provinces concerning a trans-Canada highway, and I should like to discuss that matter for a few minutes this afternoon.
Three routes have been proposed for a trans-Canada highway. The first one runs from Winnipeg to Saskatoon, Lloydiminster, Edmonton, Yellow'head pass, and from there direct to Vancouver. This one is called the Evergreen highway by those who are enthusiastic for it, and sometimes the Yellowhead highway.
The second runs from Winnipeg to Regina to Medicine Hat and from there to Calgary, Banff, and then by a circuitous route through the mountains down to Vancouver.
The third one is the southernmost route. This one goes from Winnipeg to Regina, to Medicine Hat, to Lethbridge and to Fernie, and from there to Cranbrook. Creston, Nelson, Trail, Rossland, Grand Forks, Penticton, Princeton, Hope, Vancouver, a rather direct route from Winnipeg to Vancouver.
It is my judgment, Mr. Chairman, and that of a good many others, that the one which ought to be built first is the southernmost route. I believe that ultimately Canada will find it to her advantage, for one reason or another, to have the three of these routes finished, and I would be an ardent supporter of the completion of each of them. After all, we should have one of them built first. I believe the first one should be the southernmost route.
There are a number of reasons why I take that stand. The first one is that the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have apparently looked on the southernmost route as being the most desirable transprovincial route, and have therefore devoted a great deal of attention already to the construction of highways which follow more or less the route which I have indicated. These highways, in some cases fully completed, would constitute a part of the ultimately finished highway and would therefore render the completion of the trans-Canada highway along this route less expensive than would be the highway if it followed a route such as the Evergreen route proposed, which would require the complete building of a new road.
There is another aspect of this highway which is worthy of a great deal of attention from all Canada. Because of the Chinook
belt and the influence which it has upon the area over which it blows generally, a large part of this southernmost route would be easy to keep open throughout the year. I am not contending or arguing that there are not times when a highway, even the best of highways, in Canada will be blocked and will require clearing. But taking the matter as a whole I would say it would be much easier to keep this route open the year around than any other route that may be chosen.
Another argument in favour of this route is that it is direct, the shortest possible from Winnipeg to Vancouver, being on'ly in the neighbourhood of 1,400 miles. This everyone will recognize as a real advantage.
Another advantage of this route is the high degree of industrialization which has been achieved in the past along it. If we start at Winnipeg and go out to Vancouver we shall be surprised how many well developed industries there are; not, of course, to compare with the highly developed industries in Ontario and Quebec, but even considering the fact that these are in the three or four western provinces, they are well developed. The lumbering industry has reached a fine degree of development; the mining industry has reached a high degree of development; smelting has reached a high degree of development, as has also fruit farming. Sugar manufacturing has reached a high degree of development; also canning and many other industries established from Regina, through to Vancouver.
Another aspect of this route worthy of consideration is its tourist value. It is well known to all hon. members that Canada depends in large measure for her tourist trade upon the United States. The United States people in most cases will come to Canada in cars. The result is that they will look for a highway as soon as they reach the border. If they have to go two or three hundred miles to get to the first trans-Canada highway after they cross the border, they will be apt to cross the border back again before they reach the highway; but if we have this trans-Canada highway running along the southernmost route, at no point far removed from the United States border, tourists will reach this highway rather soon after crossing the border and will be encouraged by the fact of a first-class highway to go farther into the depths of Canada.
Another aspect of this question worthy of consideration in respect of tourists is the large number of tourist attractions that are to be found along the highway. All the way from Regina west to Vancouver anyone will see items of great interest along this highway, especially after one reaches the mountains.
Supply-Mines and Resources

In the mountains he will find scenery as beauteous as is to be found anywhere in the Rocky mountains. That beauty will be found all the way along this highway. There are other items of attractions which I shall probably refer to in a while, and which would make this highway an interesting tourist attraction in its own right.
Another matter worthy of consideration in the construction of a trans-Canada highway is the population which will be found along it. It is one of the regrettable things in connection with our trans-Canada railways that they have to traverse wide spaces, sometimes hundreds of miles in extent, with hardly any people. In building this trans-Canada highway from Winnipeg to Vancouver we would find a more densely populated area than can be found in any other straight line all the way over the prairie provinces and British Columbia. Nearly everyone will agree that, by computing the population of such cities as Regina, Moose Jaw, Medicine Hat, Lethbridge, Cran-brook, Femie, Nelson, Hope, Princeton, Ross-land and other centres along that highway, we should arrive at a total of population which would render it quite obvious that we would not be building a highway for little use.
Another matter worthy of consideration is the feasibility of this highway. We shall find that at almost any point from Winnipeg right through to Vancouver the material is to be found near where the highway is to be built; gravel of high quality and other materials necessary to build a highway are at hand. This, of course, will render the construction of the highway much less expensive than it would be if we had to transport the materials from a more or less remote point.
In connection with my own constituency I think it would be well to point out, as an example of the constituencies through which this highway would pass, the truth of the general statements which I have already made. In respect of the Lethbridge federal riding the trans-Canada highway would be extremely useful. We have the sugar factories; we have the coal mines; we have canning factories and a great many other industries.
In the Lethbridge federal riding the route would be rather easy to keep open the year around compared with routes in other parts of the province. The route would go almost straight through the Lethbridge federal riding from Medicine Hat to Fernie.
As I have indicated, the industrialization which has been achieved in that area is of a high order. There are two sugar factories, one of which is at Raymond and one at Picture Butte. Each one turns out a great deal of sugar and is highly valuable in the

economy of Canada. We have ranching of a nigh order in which we produce beef and mutton in great numfofers. We have beef and mutton feeding, using the by-products which come from the sugar industry. We have three canning factories in the constituency; we have cheese factories and a considerable number of butter factories. Coal mining is extensively developed.
We have-a great many fine natural resources in the Lethbridge federal riding. We have extremely good land. We have an abundance of water for irrigation. We have four irrigation projects in the Lethbridge federal riding now supplying water to upwards of 100,000 acres of land. We have under consideration, as hon. members well know, a new irrigation project called the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project, in which it is proposed to bring 350,000 acres more of excellent land under irrigation. We have a fine climate and good water.
The tourist value of the Lethbridge federal riding is of a high order. We have the Waterton Lakes national park, one of the finest national parks in Canada. It is only a few miles from the United States border, and not far from the Logan Pass highway in that nation. Naturally people would come over from the United States to go to this park. If they knew they could reach a fine highway without too much inconvenience they would be attracted to that part of the country and' on into the inner regions of Canada. From the Waterton Lakes on to Pincher creek there is an exceedingly fine view as one drives along the road going north and looks to the lefthand at the mountain ranges. I have driven over that road many times; I never weary of looking at the great variety of mountain scenery to be found there.
We have other items such as Cardston Temple, built by the Latter Day Saints church. It is one of the most beautiful buildings to be found on the American continent.
Coming into Lethbridge federal riding is the highway which runs from the United States through Cardston straight north to connect with the Alaska highway. If we had the trans-Canada highway passing through Lethbridge it would cross the Alaska highway with all the possibilities which would accrue from that set-up. The population of Lethbridge federal riding is rather dense for a prairie constituency. We have 16.800 in the city of Lethbridge. We have a considerable number of people in the smaller towns like Cardston. Raymond, Magrath, Warner, Milk River. Taber and various other towns.

Supply-Mines and Resources
The provincial government of Alberta is spending a great deal of money this year on the building of highways in that area. It is proposed at an early day to finish off the highway from Medicine Hat to Lethbridge and to continue that highway from Lethbridge through Cardston to Waterton Lakes park, which would fit in exactly with the picture I was outlining a minute or two ago. There is under construction and soon to be completed by the Alberta government one of the finest pieces of highway to be found in western Canada, namely, that from Coutts to Lethbridge; that is to be a modern, standard highway. This highway would, of course, be tributary to the trans-Canada highway as it passed through Lethbridge. This fact would indicate how desirable the trans-Canada highway through that area would be, because a great many other subsidiary highways would cross and recross the highway, making it highly valuable from the point of view of tourists and from the point of view of general usefulness to the people. I could say a great deal more about this route for the trans-Canada highway, because I have given considerable attention to it, but I feel it would not be advisable for me to hold up the committee any longer. I should just like to offer a few suggestions and draw a few conclusions from what I have already said.
In the first place, I believe the trans-Canada highway route should be planned at the present time. All four western provinces are today spending a great deal of money and taking a good deal of interest in this highway. If the federal government, through the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, were to approach the ministers of public works of the four western provinces and suggest that they have, with him, a round-table discussion to determine what would be the most desirable route and what would be the most desirable standard of highway to build, I am sure that the building programme which is in progress at the present time could be fitted into the broad general scheme in a way which would be impossible at any future time I would, therefore, suggest that this highway be completely planned not later than September, 1947. The route should be finished not later than 1948. The construction of this highway has been long overdue. It should have been built before the war. It could not very well be built during the war. It should not be deferred any longer. Now is the time. This highway should be completed and in perfect running order from Winnipeg through to Vancouver not later than the end of 1948. I suggest that should be the goal set by the federal government.
The matter of costs enters in. It must be borne in mind that the four western provinces, not being highly industralized, do not have extensive resources from which to draw revenue. Neverthless they have great potentialities, and the contribution of wTealth which they make to the dominion as a whole is great. It w'ould, therefore, seem entirely appropriate that we suggest that the federal government pay one-half of the total cost of constructing this highway. Of course the provinces have been spending money on this highway for a great many years, but I would be of opinion that the provinces would feel quite happy with the situation if the federal government undertook to pay fifty per cent of the co-t, from January 1, 1946, up to the time w'hen the highway was finished, of the roads which would come to form that highway. That is, the federal government would say to the provinces, "Turn in a bill to us, certified and itemized, showing horv much money you have spent since January 1, 1946, on the highways which will be incorporated into this trans-Canada highway. We will give you a dollar for each dollar you have spent since January 1, 1946 along this highway; then we will pay fifty per cent of the cost of this highway for the future." There will be those who will feel that would not be a wise expenditure of public money, but there are reasons why that might be the most advantageous expenditure of public money which could be considered at the present time in the matter of transportation.
I shall say no more at the present time, Mr. Chairman, but I would commend most earnestly to the minister that he give the most careful consideration at the earliest possible day to the planning and construction of a trans-Canada highway which will run across western Canada from Winnipeg to Regina, to Medicine Hat to Lethbridge and from Lethbridge through the Crowsnest pass to Nelson and Hope, British Columbia, and on to Vancouver.

Before the committee proceeds farther, I would move that it rise, report progress and ask leave to sit later this day.
Progress reported.

On the order;
Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 364, an act to amend the criminal code.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A message was received yesterday from the senate informing this house that the

Supply-Mines and Resources
senate hadi passed Bill No. 364, an act to amend the criminal code, with amendments. A list of the amendments will be found at page 774 of the Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, July 10. A large number of amendments are proposed. They are all acceptable to the government with the exception of two. The two amendments which are not acceptable are the second and the fifteenth. The second amendment, by language which is not complete or accurate, seeks to restore the section to the form in which it was introduced in this house in the first instance. There was lengthy discussion of that amendment in the house, and it was the feeling of the house that it should not stand in the form in which it was introduced. Therefore the government has come to the conclusion that it should not accept that amendment of the senate. I may say that I am of the opinion that possibly the section, in the form in which it passed this house, is susceptible of some improvement; and I am convinced that the section, in the form in which it passed the senate, is susceptible of improvement. It would appear to me that the section would be the appropriate subject of a conference between managers of the two houses, and it would be agreeable to me if the other house took the necessary steps to bring such conference about. As I understand the rules, this would be done if they insist on their amendments. In any event I feel I have no option but to move that this amendment be not concurred in.
The second amendment is the fifteenth amendment which is in relation to a serious matter. It makes certain acts murder which are not now murder; and, if I understand the amendment correctly, goes farther in that direction than does the section as passed by the house. The government does not feel prepared to accept that amendment.

Would the minister mind
telling us what they did?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section amended is
section 260 of the criminal code, which states:
In case of treason and the other offences against the king's authority and person mentioned in part II, piracy and offences deemed to be piracy, escape or rescue from prison or lawful custody, resisting lawful apprehension, murder, rape, forcible abduction, robbery, burglary or arson, culpable homicide is also murder, whether the offender means or not death to ensue, or knows or not that death is likely to ensue.
Then follow paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d); and (d) is the amendment we inserted in this house:
(d) if he uses any weapon for the purpose of facilitating the commission of any of the offences in this section mentioned, or the flight of the 
offender upon the commission or attempted commission thereof, and death ensues as a consequence of such use.
After all, this was an important amendment which extends the English law, which, if I understand the authorities, would make such an offence manslaughter rather than murder in certain instances; but the senate amendment goes farther and substitutes for (d) the following words:
(d) if he uses or has in his possession any weapon and death ensues as a consequence of its use.
The element of intent is taken from the section as passed by this house. The words "for the purpose of facilitating the commission of any of the offences in this section mentioned, or the flight of the offender upon the commission or attempted 'commission thereof" are omitted, it being deemed, I imagine, that it might be very difficult for the crown to prove intent in those cases. It is my opinion that, the matter being of such importance, probably proof of intent should be necessary when we are making a case murder which otherwise would be manslaughter.
And what is the minister moving?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this house disagrees with their second and fifteenth amendments to the Bill No. 364, an act to amend the criminal code, for the following reasons:
"In the first case the amendment which is sought to be made by the senate is in language which has already been rejected by the house and which for this reason the house cannot accept.
In the second case, that is their fifteenth amendment, the amendment extends the operation of section 260 of the act beyond what the House of Commons contemplated or is willing to accept."

Is the minister dealing
with the other amendments now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are agreeing to all the
others.
Motion agreed to.
