130. Departmental administration, $183,177

I should like to draw to the attention of the government the necessity of doing something in order to provide roads. I am sure we have all been in the United States and have had the experience of feeling ashamed when our friends ask us when we are going to build highways in Canada. Not only do we lose a great deal of east and west traffic that we might have from the United States; we also lose a great deal of our own traffic. Man}'- of us have been guilty of hitting south as fast as possible in order to use the United States highways to make the trans-continental. I have hit for the closest port to take advantage of the concrete highways that one finds everywhere in the United States. We lose a great deal of our own money, which Canadians might be spending here, and we lose traffic that we might have in the tourist trade.
There is another aspect of this matter that has not yet been considered. When talking about transportation we must think in terms of railways, airways and highways. We would not dream of making any particular area, apart from the rest of Canada, pay for the railway passing through that territory, because all Canada pays for Canada's railways, and the operating and buliding costs are spread over the entire system. When considering a trans-Canada highway we must share the costs and not leave it entirely to the particular province through which the highway passes. When we consider the concentration of population in central Canada, for various reasons, we must come to the point where we spread the cost of building highways right across the country and absorb it as a nation.
In the west, as I need not remind the minister, our settlement is based on our rainfall, and we must have larger farming units. Where I live you cannot make a living on less than a half-section. You would not attempt to farm less than 300 or 400 acres; in fact, a section, or 600 acres, is the usual unit where I live. This means that we are bound, by our climate and geography, to have a smaller population than Ontario or Quebec; and if you force the province to bear the cost of building highways, if you tie it to the motor licence fee, your expenditure will be limited, because, if you have a small population, as we have in Saskatchewan, then the number of cars you have will be comparatively small; so

Supply-Mines and Resources

will the volume of gasoline and, in turn, the gasoline tax which will form the basis of revenue for the building of highways. Therefore, if you tie yourself to the number of cars and the number of people, and force the province to bear the entire cost, then it will be a long time before you have the kind of highways that we should have in a trans-Canada hook-up.
I should not like to say that we should have only one trans-Canada highway. I should not like to say that you should put it through my constituency, although, if you utilize the hardsurfaced road that already exists, the only paved highway, in Saskatchewan is in the path of my constituency, the one running between Winnipeg and Regina and going on through Moose Jaw and Swift Current. Number one, which is our best highway and the only one which has black top, and which has the heaviest population running alongside the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway from the oldest settlements, runs through the most heavily populated and the best built-up part of the province. It happens to run through my constituency, but I would not urge the government to build a highway merely because I happen to represent that area. But this is the highway which the province keeps open the longest. It has less snow than the northern route. The province has maintained this as the last highway to close and the first one to open in the spring, and as one listens to the weather reports, as we all do in the winter broadcasts, they always quote No. 1 as open when the others are closed.
I think we should try to have more than one highway; we should assist the provinces to have feeders running north and south, because, if we are to route traffic from the United States and Ontario to the prairie provinces, we shall have to establish some north and south highways too. But if you are thinking of the cost, I would imagine that the federal government would be interested in utilizing the best existing road to get the best highway established as quickly as possible. If they are doing that, then the number one, between Brandon and Regina, is the best existing road. It has black top through a part of it now, and it would be the easiest to maintain because it would have the least snow, and it already has a certain standard.
I would therefore ask the minister to consider building a road that we shall not have to apologize for. When you talk about roads in my province people all say, "What roads?" We really have no roads worthy of the name, when you consider the highways they have in every part of the United States. In January

I travelled to the gulf of Mexico and Florida, and never saw a gravel road anywhere, and in many cases there was a four-lane highway. In our country gravel is considered a good road. It is time we moved up our standards and had a real highway from one end of Canada to the other, which would bear the kind of traffic worthy of a great, rich and growing nation like Canada.

I do not think I can add to what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said. We may not always agree with her, but no one could express the opinion of every Canadian on this subject better than she did just now. I am going to speak purely from the tourist point of view and, if you like, from the selfish point of view of dollars and cents. Last year we had $232 million brought into Canada through the tourist trade. Well, if we ship our lumber, wheat and everything else something is going out of our country, whereas if we bring in United States money through the tourist traffic we are taking nothing out of the country.
Naturally I am a little privileged in this connection, coming as I do from the most beautiful part of Canada, the Fraser valley. They even look at the flying saucers. We have something there. I believe the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is right. Last year I drove home, taking twenty days and going 6,000 miles through the United States. If hon. members will stop talking I will drive home again in a day or two all through the United States; and why am I driving through the United States? Because they have the roads. And I will spend all the money I have to spend in the United States. We are asking tourists to come here. Our scenery is the one thing we have to sell which takes nothing out of the country, but we do not provide the tourists with the highways they are used to. I do not know anything about Saskatchewan, but I know something about my own province, which is adjacent to the state of Washington. If we can build roads, the connecting links from the United States, we certainly have not done so. The roads that we expect United States tourists to travel on when they come into Canada are a disgrace. Vancouver is the third city in Canada, with the most vocal mayor on the North American continent, and we have a cow trail leading into that city.
The most vocal in the world.

We expect United States tourists to come in and travel on that trail. Why should the province be expected to build that highway when it would bring money into the country at a time when we

Supply-Mines and Resources
are hearing so much about foreign exchange, and are being told that we cannot d,o anything about that situation? Apparently the federal government is afraid to spend money to build highways. I believe it is good common-sense business to expend money in the construction of highways across Canada that would connect with the United States border. This would encourage the tourist traffic and enable us to sell them something which cannot be equalled in any other part of the world, our Canadian scenery.

I have a few words to add
in support of what has been said already with regard to the construction of a trans-Canada highway. It seems to me that in this day and age good highways are almost indispensable. Modern civilization is almost wholly dependent upon good transportation. To build roads anywhere in Canada is an expensive undertaking, and the completion of the trans-Canada highway would be a costly venture for the provinces to attempt. Thar, is wli3' I advocate that something should be done, preferably at this session, but at least by next session, to expedite the construction of a trans-Canada highway through the western provinces at the earliest possible moment. This should be on the basis of a fifty per cent contribution by the federal government, because I believe it is generally considered that the trans-Canada highway should be a national undertaking and not left to the individual provinces to complete.
I may say that neither one of the highways which have been referred to in Saskatchewan runs through my constituency, but I would be inclined to favour at the moment the construction of the highway passing through Moose Jaw and Regina, The present No. 1 highway enters at Fleming and goes through to the western border where it links with the Alberta highway system. It is approximately 450 miles long, and I question if there is any place in Canada where highway construction could be carried on as cheaply. Approximately 110 miles are surfaced with what is called black top. This probably does not measure up to the standards of better highways, but it serves our purpose and is much better than the roads we have been using in past years. The rest of the highway is gravel. The government of Saskatchewan is paving some 239 miles of road this year and some of that paving will be on that particular highway. Another bit of paving will be on highway No. 39, which links up with a United States highway coming up from Minneapolis and St. Paul and passing through Weyburn. It is proposed to complete that road by 1948, and that is another reason 83166-349J
why I advocate the completion of highway No. 1. This would provide a link to the east and west for people, tourists in the main, coming from the south. They could then continue on their way into Alberta, to Banff, Calgary and Vancouver or Winnipeg to the east.
There are many other arguments in favour of the completion of the highway which I shall not go into now. Everybody knows that highways constitute a great national asset. They encourage tourists among other things. These days much of our freight is handled by trucks and good highways facilitate their movement. We have great hopes of irrigation programmes in the west. When that day comes-and I hope it will in another :.wo or three years-thousands of good people will come to southern Saskatchewan and there will be an additional need for good highways. That is another reason why we advocate the construction of a paved highway through the southern part of the province.
Saskatchewan is regarded as a prairie province with very little attraction for the tourist, but a person passing through there might be greatly surprised if he took No. 1 highway and stopped at the points of interest. For example, there is Moosomin, a town of some 2,000 people, which was the birthplace of that great Canadian, General McNaughton. Then there is the Indian Head experimental farm. I need not mention Regina, because the hon. member for that riding is capable of doing that. Moose Jaw is on that same highway, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw has told the committee a great deal about that city. There are also Swift Current and Maple Creek, both of which are famous, not only for the meat packing plants that are located there, but because of cowboys, rodeos and that sort of thing. There are a number of attractions in Saskatchewan. I appeal to the minister to get on with the job of constructing the trans-Canada highway. If it is not feasible to build both roads, let us have one at least.

I want to assure the committee that this is not a filibuster, and I want also to tell our northern Canadian neighbours that neither is it an attack on their estimable selves. We would like them to have a highway as well. I want to continue the support for a project which we believe is necessary. Other hon. members have given reasons why this highway is necessary and I agree with them. We probably need more than two trans-Canada highways, but we certainly need one immediately to follow the route of highway No. 1.
The paving of that highway is partly completed, and it is the most direct route to those
Supply-Mines and Resources

going to the third largest city in Canada located on the west coast. We believe it is the proper one to build. If that one is completed, as recommended by the hon. member for Lethbridge, by 1948, that in itself would lead to the more rapid completion of the northern highway. If feeder roads are built running north and south by the province and the municipalities that would create more demand and pressure for the northern highway. I assure you that I am not trying to create a division. As I say, the reasons why this road should be completed have been stated before. I speak with authority only for the little area I represent, but in that area we have many of the attributes mentioned by other hon. members.
I will admit that our population is not as dense as that of Toronto, Montreal or even Ottawa; in fact it is not as dense by any standard of measurement you care to use. But they are energetic and, because of that, they have created a number of interesting industries and are in the process of creating others outside of the agricultural industry which in themselves are well worth seeing. Anyone who would like to see a large flock of sheep handled by an expert shepherd and expert dogs will be well repaid for taking a trip through there. Anyone who would like to see large herds of beautiful white-faced cattle travelling and grazing over the lovely ranch lands in the Cypress hills would be well advised to take a trip through there. To see beauty one does not necessarily have to go to the mountains or to the St. Lawrence river. Come to our flax-growing areas when the flax is in bloom, and you will see no more beautiful sight as a tourist attraction. Our irrigation projects and other industries are opening up new avenues for human energy to be expended for the expansion of our country as a whole. When these things are taking place, if a highway goes through there, it will not only lend itself to tourist traffic but facilitate the development of those industries, and, by so doing, will open that particular gateway to further highways further north, as far north as it is necessary to have them.

Mr. Chairman, I have been studying the face of the minister while this discussion has been going on and trying to guess from his granite countenance whether he intends to build any highway at all. Not having been able to come to a conclusion from looking at him, I am going to address a question to him in regard to the matter. It would appear to me that there has been a sort of inter-party conspiracy to talk about a

southern highway through the dust-bowl of Canada, where there is no beauty and very little wealth.
Have you seen our girls?

I think it may be taken for granted that we all really want a highway across Canada, and perhaps more than one. I hardly expect, however, that the minister will build more than one before the next session. But if he is going to build only one I think we ought to know which one it is to be.
I want to draw to his attention that most of the beauty and most of the wealth of the western provinces lie in the northern section, and I would ask him, before building any highway across Canada, to give some thought to a trans-Canada highway via Jasper and from there on to the coast-
Over the Evergreen route.

Yes, that is the kind of route we want to get. I could speak at length on the merits of the different routes, but I do not wish to take up the time of the committee. I suggest that the minister assure us that he will at least give consideration to that route I mentioned before he plunges in any wild way into building a road to the west across Canada. I would also ask him to consider joining that road to the great Alaska highway, so that we may have a complete crossing, not only across Canada, but right up north to Nome.

I can assure my hon. friend that a great deal of consideration will be given to the matter before we build any such roads. When the decision has to be made as to the route, the provinces involved will be consulted, and an attempt will be made to reach an agreement.
That is the proper way.

If consideration is
being given to the building of a highway across this country I should like to bring out one or two points. All the transportation facilities of this country run north of the 49th parallel of latitude, so that one would think that all Canada consisted of was that northern fringe which exists north of the United States. A mistake was made originally in putting two railroads across Canada just north of the 49th parallel. They should have been laid farther north, so that feeder lines could have served them from both north and south. In view of the development that has taken place in the north and the desire of the government to develop the north I think consideration should be given to a more northerly route for a trans-

Supply-Mines find Resources
Canada highway. There is also this advantage that the grades are better through the mountains. That has been proved by the Canadian National Railways, as anyone who has taken a trip through the Crowsnest pass can see for himself. One farmer decided, after going through the pass, that if he wanted any further excitement he would run up two poles to his barn door and run up and down on them. So I would urge the minister to consider the Y'ellowhead pass route.

After listening to the remarks made by the hon. member for Cariboo, I must say a few words about the so-called dust-bowl to which he referred. I believe that in that so-called dust-bowl we have more scenery than there is in the north country. Go through one of the irrigation districts and you would think you were down here, the scenery is so beautiful. The only difference between our irrigation areas and the country down here is that our soil is much better.
The minister has been given many suggestions as to routes through the western provinces. I believe that three routes have been suggested. I feel that it should be a southern route to start with. However, in the past I have supported a route through Calgary, which, of course, is not the one that has received most support this afternoon. I believe that the highway should not be built too close to the southern part of the western provinces but should go perhaps through Calgary. We in Medicine Hat are on the "Y" of the trans-Canada highway, as the road is sure to go through there whether it branches out to Lethbridge or Calgary. The main thing is that we want a trans-Canada highway, and I am sure that Canadians generally want it as soon as they can get it. There is no reason why we should have to travel through the United States to get home from Ottawa.

The route of a trans-Canada highway west of Winnipeg naturally would cause some division between those who represent the northern portions and those who represent the southern portions of the western provinces. I think each of the routes has. some qualification, and naturally many people in the area would like to see the route through there. The Evergreen route is one which now passes through the great populous areas of these provinces in the west. I do not say that because we wish to take away from the southern routes. We should like to know from the minister whether there is any possibility of building a trans-Canada highway within three years. If the minister can give us that information, perhaps we can come to some agreement. We appreciate his statement that
when the government is deciding which route should be built or what routes shall be built through these provinces the provincial governments will be taken into consideration. Along with that they will be working on a plan which will meet with general satisfaction.

In reply to the question, the government has from time to time given assistance to the provinces in the building of highways. As far as the federal government is concerned, the decision ihas rested in part, on the level of unemployment. When the unemployment situation was beyond the power of the provinces to deal with, the government has joined with the provinces in a programme of public works. Naturally, the programme of a trans-Canada highway has had an important place in such programmes. My ihon. friend knows that a new financial agreement has been made with certain provinces, which has placed those provinces in a better financial position than previously. It has not been possible to obtain agreement with all the provinces on a programme of public development. At the moment, the government is not in a position to make any commitments as to when or whether it will join with the provinces in a programme for a trans-Canada highway.
A relief project.

Living as I do in the southern part of Alberta, and having a constituency which is in the foothills of the Rockies, it seems to me that I, too, should get into this debate on an appropriate all-Canada highway. I must confess that I was a little shocked and surprised to hear the minister almost confess that a trans-Canada highway was dependent upon the next depression when unemployment would be a problem.
If I may reply, I would say that I am astonished that my hon. friend suggests that the provinces could not possibly build any highway without federal help.

I did not suggest that; somebody else may have done so. But I am shocked to think that the present government is looking forward to doing something in respect of highways by a method of relief camps. That is a vital principle. However I do not suppose that any public moneys can be spent for public works any more advantageously or appropriately than for an all-Canada highway, and one that is adequate to maintain real tourist traffic and attract that tourist traffic to Canada.
Not so long ago I remember reading one of the reports of the senate committee on tourist traffic. I was really amazed to find
Supply-Mines and Resources

the evidence submitted to that committee showed that there was more money coming into Canada from tourist trade than through all our foreign trade combined. When we think of that it is amazing. Our government seems to spend a great deal of. time, energy, effort and argument on the building up of foreign trade. It has its trade commissioners in almost every part of the globe to maintain trade at a huge expense, and yet it is a bigger business for Canada to deal in tourist trade and tourist attractions which bring in more money than all our foreign trade combined. That was the evidence brought out in the senate committee. That is quite a thing. Therefore we have need to think of this highway in the light of our tourist trade.
I have heard arguments sometimes that all hon. members will want such a highway to go through their own constituencies. I do not have to argue the point very much because I know very well it is going through mine. There is no doubt at all. When anyone thinks of tourist trade throughout Canada itself, he does not think of it without thinking in terms of Banff, Lake Louise, the Columbia ice fields, the Windermere highway, and so forth.
The hon. member for Cariboo says that it should go through Cariboo. I know that when I talk with people and mention Cariboo they say, "Who is he?" Or if I should mention the Evergreen highway, they do not know anything about that. If I should mention the Yellowhead highway they will say: "We have heard of redheads; we have heard of roundheads; we have heard of fatheads; we have heard of all sorts of heads, but a yellowhead is a new one on us." But if we just mention Banff, Lake Louise, the Columbia ice fields or Windermere or even the Prince of Wales ranch everybody knows where it is. People sometimes ask me where I am from. If I give them the name of my own town they do not know where that is; but if I say, "You have heard of the Prince of Wales ranch," they will say "yes." When I say, "well, he is my neighbour", they then know where I live.
The southernmost highway is bound to connect with those great tourist attractions therefore I know it is going through there anyway. The minister should get busy on this. He will be able to make a lot of money for this country if he does. Do not leave it, please, for a hand-out in the way of dole when it comes to relief.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.
130. Departmental administration, $183,173.

I wish to make a few brief remarks in connection with this item, and to support the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lethbridge and others. I think there is general agreement with regard to the necessity for the building of a trans-Canada highway and the improvement of a trans-Canada highway system. If you will read the history of the Roman empire, Mr. Chairman, of 'the B-itish empire, and of the United States, I thing you will find that the development of any country depends upon the development of a satisfactory highway system. If you read Roman history you will find that, when the Romans occupied Britain, the Roman consuls and other officials of that kind pointed to the fact that if they were to develop Britain they would have to develop the highways of that country. The same applies to the British empire. With regard to India particularly, I remember reading some remarks made by one of the prominent officials governing India who, in the British House of Commons, pointed out that the development of India must be based on the development of the highways. The same thing goes for the United States. Quite recently the United States passed* a large vote for the development of highways by the cooperation of the federal and state governments. In the last month or so, even the small republic of Mexico has voted S500,000,000 for the development of trans-Mexico highways. I think there is general agreement that we need to develop our trans-Canada highway system. I do not believe there is any opposition to that from one end1 of Canada to the other, if we are to develop our natural resources and take advantage of our tourist possibilities in the future. In that connection I wish to quote the report of the senate committee of last year on the tourist traffic:
Almost every witness appearing before your committee stressed the need of better roads if tourist traffic was to expand. The prevailing opinion was that Canada had unlimited tourist attractions. To make them accessible, allweather highways were necessary and federal assistance would be required to assist in the provision of the main arteries of approach, particularly from the United States.
I do not think there is any question about that. As a member representing a British Columbia riding, I want to deal with aspects
Supply-Mines and Resources

of the question that refer particularly to my province. I say without hesitation that if British Columbia is to be satisfactorily serviced with highway transportation we shall require to have three routes through the mountain areas of that province: First, the southern, transprovincial route; second, the Kicking Horse pass or Big Bend route, and, thirds, the Yellowhead pass route. In this connection, while we believe that one of these routes should receive priority when it comes to construction, I do not think we shall be satisfactorily served, owing to the nature of the country, until all three routes are constructed.
This evening I wish to refer briefly to the southern transprovincial highway between Hope in British Columbia and Lethbridge in Alberta. As far as the physical possibility of building the route is concerned, that has been proved, because we now have a highway of a sort in existence between Hope and Lethbridge. There might be some criticism of that route, because at one point at the present time it has to cross the Cascade mountains at an elevation of 5,400 feet, and the Rossland summit at an elevation of 4,400 feet. As a solution of those two difficulties, however, first of all we have the suggestion by the Rossland board of trade that arrangements should be made for a diversion into United States territory for a distance of five miles in depth and thirty miles in length between Rossland and Grand Forks, British Columbia; or, second, there is the possibility of building a tunnel to reduce the elevation to which the present highway goes in the Cascade mountains.
That is a very small matter when one comes to compare it with the possibilities which would result from the development of the whole highway. As far as the Big Bend or Kicking Horse highway is concerned, that is much more difficult to keep open under winter conditions, owing to the greater fall of snow, than the southern transprovincial highway. Further, in support of the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge, I would say that the distance between Winnipeg and Vancouver is shortened by the use of this highway to 1,400 miles.
When it comes to the question of population, anyone who has studied the population of British Columbia realizes that, with the exception of the coast cities, the great bulk of the population resides south of the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway, and if this highway were built it would serve a population of about 125,000. In addition, there are certain definite economic advantages. Along the route of that highway we have the smelter 
of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, which last year produced $60,000,000 worth of mineral and other products. In addition, we have various other subsidiary industries in connection with the production of poles and, in the near future, the production of pulp throughout that area. As far as mining is concerned, if the road between Lethbridge and Hope were built it would serve one of the richest mining districts in British Columbia. As far as the lumbering industry is concerned, between Lethbridge and Hope at the present time about 200.000,000 feet of lumber are produced, in addition to large quantities of cedar poles which are supplied to markets in Minneapolis and New York, as well as other timber products. As far as agriculture is concerned, taking the Kootenay, Arrow lakes and Okanagan valleys we have a total production of fruit products amounting to some $25,000,000. As far as tourist advantages are concerned, we are very close to the international boundary. Our feeder roads would connect with United States roads and permit the influx of large numbers of tourists who wish to visit the national parks; who wish to see the beauties of the Cascade range, the Monaskee range, the Selkirk range and the Rocky mountain range and also the many hot springs that abound throughout the district. The fishing and hunting in the area between Lethbridge and Hope is unexcelled in any part of Canada.
There is no question but that the development of this route will service the greatest commercial and industrial area in the interior of British Columbia; and, for the money expended, will produce greater returns than the development of any other area in British Columbia at the present time. Last year the government of British Columbia expended some $600,000 on the development of this route between Hope and the Alberta border of the province, and this year they are expending some $100,000.
We in the southern part of British Columbia realize that, before our province can be adequately serviced w'ith trans-Canada highways, we must have the completion of the three routes I have mentioned. I believe all three should be included in the plans for the construction of trans-Canada highways in the future. But because of the large population in the interior of British Columbia south of the main line, because of the large industrial, agricultural and lumbering developments, we believe the route between Lethbridge and Hope should receive priority. The construction and improvement of this route have the support of all the boards of trade between

Supply-Mines and Resources
Vancouver and Lethbridge, of all the service organizations, of all the farmer organizations and all other groups within this area, and I urge early action by the government on this project. I urge that the minister give serious consideration to the opinion of these people. As was evidenced this afternoon, we have the support of hon. members from Alberta, from Saskatchewan and from Manitoba. So far as the extension of the trans-Canada highway is concerned, I say the southern provincial highway through the mountains should have priority.
I urge that the minister consider on a fifty-fifty basis early action on the southern route in British Columbia, and that, in addition to that, preparation and plans be made for the development of the Kicking Horse pass and Yellowhead routes.

I would call to the hon. member's attention the fact that, whereas . Canada has not made provision for the construction of the trans-Canada highway at this time, it has introduced in the supplementary estimates a vote of 8200,000 to commence the surfacing of the Windermere highway, which is a start in the direction my hon. friend is advocating.
I am glad to hear that.

Mr. Chairman-, it is agreed on all sides that a programme of highway construction for Canada is needed at this time. I- have received a number of communications from different organizations in my constituency, and I feel I should say a word with respect to this particular project. I am not at all opposed- to the construction of highways across Canada, whether it be by the southern route or the northern route. But. inasmuch as the southern route would go through the most densely populated part of my constituency, I feel naturally that that highway should have priority in construction. When that work is done we should look toward the building of other highways; whether they should be through the northerly or the central part of the province remains to be . seen.
In the riding which I have the honour to represent, and through which this southern highway now runs we have a highly industrialized area. We have the coal mining district of the Crowsnest pass; we have the hard-rock mining of Kimberley, the area from which all the ore is extracted for the Trail smelter.
We have, too, a great deal of lumbering in that part of the country, which is contiguous to the southern highway. Not only that, but it runs through a highly productive fruit belt
known as the Creston valley area, in which some of the finest fruit of British Columbia is produced.
One hon. member this afternoon tried to leave the impression with the committee that all the scenic beauty is in northern British Columbia. I can only say that he has not yet travelled through the southern area, because, if he did, he would learn that his remarks were just sour grapes. The scenic beauty of southern British Columbia stands unrivalled.
Entering this area is one of the main highway routes from the United States, crossing the international boundary at Kingsgate. We have a splendid road system through that area, bringing the tourists into the famous Kootenay national park, and the Yoho and Banff national parks. Not only so, but in the district contiguous to this southern highway is one of the big-game areas of British Columbia. It is the area to which tourists and big-game hunters are coming from all parts of the world, whether they are looking for moose, elk, or grizzly bear.
They just pass through there on their way to the Cariboo.

They do not pass through, because they do not need to go beyond the area about which I have -been speaking.
We already have the southern route through the Crowsnest pass. All we ask the minister to do is to give consideration to the standardizing of this particular highway. So much has already been constructed, and I know others have spoken of the service which this highway could render.
Let me repeat that I am not opposed to the construction of other highways as they become necessary, but anyone passing through the southern part of British Columbia will find that that is the most densely populated area. This particular highway is now serving that area, and greater development lies ahead. I should think that everything in the area about which I have spoken would commend itself to the department, when it is considering the construction of highways.
I am pleased to know that the minister is considering highway development and construction; and we feel sure that when the merits of these various localities are fully considered the southern highway will stand foremost in their consideration.

I appreciate the fact that hon. members in the committee are anxious to make headway, and I shall be brief. However I wish to impress upon the government the need for an enlightened attitude toward
Supply-Mines and Resources

the building of highways. It seems to me that a trans-Canada highways policy is decades overdue. One remembers the golden age of Canada's expansion and development which followed the building of the railway systems some sixty or seventy years ago, when the Canadian Pacific railway was built across the country, followed by the Grand Trank and the Canadian Northern. The terrific impact of motor transport improvement and development compels a changed federal attitude toward the building of durable highways, something which is as important as the development of ports, harbours and foreign trade.
Perhaps the corduroy roads of the early pioneers were sufficient for those days. They made it possible for (those early settlers to get to the store, to the church or to the school. But we have passed the horse and buggy days-never to return, I (hope. I maintain that the provinces are not in a position adequately to finance road building today, any more than they were able six decades ago to finance the building of the railways. For example, only seven per cent of the population of Canada lives in Saskatchewan, but in that province is found thirty-eight per cent of the road surface. It is ridiculous to think that that province can maintain a standard of road building as high as that of other more densely populated areas.
This afternoon we discussed immigration. We need immigration, for a variety of reasons, not the least of which is the giving of more traffic to our railways so that they may be more self-sustaining. The same might be said with respect to the development of super-highways. I see no reason why immigrant labour forces languishing in displaced persons camps in Europe could not be transplanted to (this country, so that a benevolent government in Canada could give its citizens a highways system in keeping with the place Canada is expected to hold in the commonwealth of nations. The immigrants could help in the building of these highways.
I should like to be more specific with regard to the type of programme that we should have. When we passed the defence estimates the other night I drew the attention of the Minister of National Defence to certain gaps in our defence programme. We are spending a quarter of a billion dollars in the way that we followed in previous years. We are still carrying on the barrack-room type of training of our troops. If we are really going to defend this country we must be realistic. Those of us who have been in the services appreciate what it means to have a highly mobile force. We are satisfied that the railways do not permit the
rMr. Probe.]
moving of huge supplies of materials and large masses of men at a rapid rate from place to place. From the point of view of mobility we are defenceless, because the railways are vulnerable at their marshalling yards located at points like Winnipeg. If they were put out of working order it would immobilize hundreds of miles of defence regions.
We should have ancillary highway sytems. Standard or superstandard highways should be built and maintained, at least partly at the expense of the Department of National Defence. The engineers in the services could obtain worth-while training by actually constructing these highways. One system of highways right across the country should be built and maintained by the Department of National Defence as part of our defence programme. In addition-I am not speaking in terms of local patriotism, because Regina is on what is officially considered the trans-Canada highway-to that one main artery for the movement of vehicles to be maintained by the Department of National Defence-shall we say this would be highway No. 1?-there should be a colonization highway system to open up those areas of Canada so rich in natural wealth-these were mentioned bjr the hon. member for Cariboo-and this should be the joint responsibility of the federal government through the Department of Mines and Resources or the Department of Reconstruction and the provincial governments.
I think this is a practical suggestion, because it would permit the movement of troops from the defence point of view and would also tap our natural resources and open up colonization areas which are still unsettled. We should then have arterial roads running, from the international border, roads which would link up with the excellent United States roads, through to our northland, These roads could be financed by the provinces perhaps with loans from the federal government. If necessary, tolls could be charged on these lines originating at the border and running northward until capital costs wer* realized.
The programme I envisage is one main motor highway to be maintained by the Department of National Defence. Then there would be another main east-west built jointly by the provincial governments and the dominion Department of Mines and Resources or the Department of Reconstruction, for the purposes of opening up new areas and giving impetus to immigration into this country. Then there would be feeder lines running north and south to our rich lake lands and mineral resources which, would be constructed, in, the first instance by means of funds lent to the provinces and then paid for, if such were felt

Supply-Mines and Resources
necessary, by means of tolls. We would then have a comprehensive over-all system which, in terms of motor transport, would take us out of the horse and buggy days or, what is worse, the oxcart stage.

Item agreed to.
Mines and geology branch-
131. Branch administration, $40,068.

First, I should like to
congratulate the department upon the good work it has done in the discovery of oil along the Athabaska river. Last session we voted some thousands of dollars to continue the drilling for oil in this area. In January las; I read in the Windsor Star, than which there is no better paper in Canada, a most interesting article in connection with the work of Doctor Hume, one of the departmental geologists. This reads in part:
Liquid bitumen of high quality, from three to 52 feet in thickness, carrying from 12 to 18 per cent bitumen by weight, in bituminous sands up to 220 feet thick, and tentatively considered to contain from 400 to 500 million barrels of bitumen. has been developed by recent diamond drilling over a two square mile area.
A company, I believe called Oil Sands Limited, has found equally large reservoirs of oil near that same area along the Athabaska river. The acting minister is familiar with the production of oil from the sands of the Athabaska river and he knows of the worldwide search for oil. The department of interior of the United States recently called together a conference of oil geologists, engineers and oil production men from all over the country, to ascertain whether all the known fields in the United States were being searched and whether full development was being carried on. As a result, the announcement was then made by the department that it was calculated that the total oil resources of the United States were about twenty-one billion barrels and that the known resources of the world were about forty-two billion barrels. Those are not very great resources, and therefore it is imperative that our Department of Mines and Resources should use every effort-and I believe it is doing so-to discover new sources. We have as good geologists and oil engineers in our department as there are in any other geological department and we should use eveiy effort to try to find more oil.
At the moment people in Toronto-and I presume this would apply to other cities-are fearful over being able to obtain sufficient oil for their home furnaces, not to mention business requirements. I tried recently to buy four oil burners for buildings which I own. I assume I could have bought the burners,
but the large company with which I deal- I believe in dealing with companies which are strong-advised me that they were unable to take on any more customers. The situation is really acute, and I hope the minister will be able to reassure the committee that there will be a greater production of oil in Canada.
In Washington they are making every effort to follow up every possible method for the synthetic production of oil from coal and oil shale. I see in their reports that they say there is more than half the coal in all the world in the United States. Canada, too, has an almost inexhaustible supply of coal, great coal beds that have not been touched at all, and if oil is to be produced from coal there is no reason why our department through its plant on Booth street, for which we shall be voting a sum of money shortly, should not make every effort to ascertain the most feasible method of extracting oil from coal to make it available for use in furnaces throughout Canada.
To me the problem before this country seems tremendous. If any other country-I shall not mention which one-wanted to make an attack on Canada, all it would have to do would be to shut off our coal and oil supplies and we would be through. Yet we have vast quantities of coal in this country, and according to departmental reports we have in the oil sands more than five times as much oil as there is in all the rest of the world combined. So I hope that some method will be developed whereby oil can be extracted from the sands. If as Doctor Hume's report says we have vast beds of pure bitumen, the minister must know that is something worth while. It is no great trick to take the oil out of bitumen, and if we have that quantity of bitumen there, there is no reason why we should not produce oil from it.
One company in Edmonton on whom I called last January and will likely call again next January, told me that they owned a property approximately 35 miles in length along the Athabaska river on the east side, three-quarters of a mile in depth back from the river and 250 feet in depth in the ground. Their tests show that they have a large volume of almost pure bitumen in vast quantity. During the war the company went to Washington and got in touch with the Reconstruction Finance Corporation for an investment of $30,000,000. I know the minister is familiar with that, because I saw a letter from Washington saying that if the company could get his approval the Reconstruction Finance Corporation would invest the $30,000,000 to develop these oil resources. They should be
Supply-Mines and Resources

developed. If the departmental engineers were correct-and I have no reason to doubt that; this country spent very large sums of money to enable them to make their investigations during the war-there are vast quantities of oil up there. It cannot be extracted by any simple ABC method; but there is a proper method of extracting the oil, and after forty or fifty years of dealing with it and parliament having voted during the last few years quite a few hundreds of thousands of dollars for the construction of a small pilot plant on Booth street, I think it is high time that those engineers brought something forward. They are taking a long while to do so. Methods are known by which the oil can be extracted.
I had a letter yesterday from Utah-I am going there on my trip west-where they are making a great success with the McClave method which was developed by the very same man who had been in control of the Abasand plant at Fort McMurray. It was said that the plant at Fort McMurray was burned down. There was little to show that it achieved anything. But the McClave method is proving a success. I have a letter from the oil people at Vernal in Utah to visit Vernal to see their success in extracting oil from oil sands, and when I return home in the fall of the year I shall know a whole lot more about it.
I think it is up to this department, laying everything else to one side, to exert itself, and speedily, in defence of the homes of this country by developing some method of extracting oil from bitumen. In the report in the Windsor Star which I quoted, the department itself says there is a large volume to start with, four to five hundred million barrels of bitumen.
The other company to which I referred was ,lil Sands Limited. I saw their construction plans, which included a pipeline. They were going to extract the oil out of the sands and pipe it to Edmonton, which I think is the right thing to do, and construct a refinery at Edmonton. Their plans called for the delivery of 8,000 to 10,000 barrels of bitumen a day at Edmonton, there to be refined into oil. What I wish to impress on the minister is this, although he knows a lot about this, perhaps more than any of us, to push along his engineers and geologists and tell them to get on with the business as rapidly as they can. The Alberta government is making every effort to do likewise. When I was in Edmonton last winter I went to the university and saw their small pilot plant and discussed the question with their professors. They feel they have a good production method. The trouble

has been to get a refinery but they expect to have a refinery in operation down the river. In any event, no matter who does it, the Alberta government, Oil Sands Limited, or Abasand if it is ever resurrected-I believe it is out of commission now-they should push on and make every effort to overcome this country's oil fuel problem. For thirty-five or forty years this department has said and has been putting out circulars stating that there is a lot of oil up there and I think it is pretty nearly time we started to get some results. We cannot go on buying oil indefinitely from the United States. If that country ever shut off our supply we should be through.
There is another part of Canada in which there is oil. I spent some time in Hillsborough, New Brunswick, last September. I do not know if the minister was there but they spoke of him at different times. There I saw quite a substantial oil field with eighteen wells in operation. They were producing only seven barrels of oil a day per well but that is the United States average. There are 30,000 paying wells in the United States producing seven barrels each per day.
It is mostly fuel gas, is it not?

Yes, they produce gas and oil; they ship the gas to Moncton and heat the city with gas. I heard down there that the gentleman who owned it lived in England and that he was not well. I have since heard from the hon. member for Royal that he has passed away. I heard also from other sources that the whole field and plant have been taken over by the Shell Oil interests-I am not sure that that is so-and that they are producing a lot more oil than was produced a year ago. If that is so, then there is another field, and goodness knows the maritime provinces need something like that to put them on the map. I should like to see them strike three or four big gushers down there that would put them on the map so far as oil production goes.
I do not want to delay the committee any longer, but I felt it my duty to talk about this. I know a good deal about it myself. I hope when I come back from Utah, I have a better report that a real improvement has been made in the method of extraction. I am going to suggest to the department that they communicate with the company. If they do not know the name of the company I shall be glad to give it to them. I suggest that they communicate with the company and get a report from the geologists and engineers down there, showing that they are getting results. I suggest that they send one or two geologists

Supply-Mines and Resources
and engineers down there to see what they are doing. The fact is that we have to do something. If we have a resource to develop we should be making every effort to develop it. I am not going to find any fault with anything that has been done in the past. That does not do any good. I want to encourage those in authority to go forward, to look up and do the best they can to provide oil either from oil wells or from oil sands or coal. If the method th^it is now in operation in the United States for taking oil out of coal is to be used, and we have to get oil production from coal, let us do so. The fact is, we must become self-sufficient and independent so far as oil is concerned.
Anyone can visualize just what a tremendous thing it would mean in Canada. I said a moment ago that I recently tried to buy four oil burners. I could have obtained the burners, but the company told me they could not get the oil. There are many thousands of people in Canada in the same position. The production of oil burners would bring a lot of business; the production of pumps, tanks, steel for oil tanks and so on would mean a lot to this country. This country would bound along fast if we could only get oil, and this would be one source of production. Then we could also have oil produced from coal and shale as they are doing in Utah and Colorado. There is a lot of shale in New Brunswick. I know the acting minister is an engineer and knows a lot about these things. He knows more about them than the ordinary cabinent minister does. Our trouble in Canada is that we have appointed men to cabinet positions who are not always familiar with what they direct. Some of them do, but not all of them. I am not referring to the present minister. I know the acting minister does know something about these things. I suggest to him that he look carefully into all these problems of oil production and encourage his engineers and geologists, who are as good as the best, to put our country on the map in all these various items to which I have referred.

I should like to say a few words on this subject. As hon. members know, the Department of Mines and' Resources has a strong geology branch, and particularly strong in the matter of oil geology. The results that are now being obtained in Alberta are due in no small part 'to the study made by the officers of this department, and to their cooperation with private industry.
I quite agree with my hon. friend that one of the great weaknesses in the Canadian
economy is the lack of sufficient oil to support our economy. That lack is even more serious than the lack of well distributed supplies of coal. During the war years the government spent about two and a half million dollars in a thorough exploration of the Abasand situation; that is, an exploration of the tar sands of northern Alberta. The department had been working on the problem in a small way for some twenty years. It was recognized that, when war broke out, the need for oil would be paramount. Exploration was speeded up. The exploration brought some excellent results. A thorough drilling of the location resulted in delivering, and mapping areas high in bitumen, areas that had considerable quantities of free bitumen. The programme has also perfected the process for separating bitumen from the sand. Unfortunately, just as the work was being finished, a fire burned down the separation plant and brought a halt to the investigation; but at that time practically all the results that had been hoped for had been achieved. We knew where the oil is located; we knew the approximate cost of recovery; we know a satisfactory process for separating oil from the sands. The department then decided that it had done its work as far as acquiring data on tar sands is concerned. The department was successful in making a verjr satisfactory agreement with the owners of the property under which, if oil is ever produced, or if other valuable substances are ever produced1 from the area, the government will recover all the money it has spent in the area. The government then retired from the tar sand situation.
The situation regarding petroleum, as it seems to be developing at the moment, is that it is expected that petroleum from wells will not last indefinitely. At the present time supply is below demand. That is a temporary situation which it may take two years to correct. The fact seems to be that drilling and development work have not kept up with the sharp increase in post-war demand. It seems to be the view of industry that in time, not in the time of myself or my hon. friend, oil will become scarce to the point where hydrogenation will be a practical development and when the tar sands will be a very valuable source of oil. At the moment, oil from tar sands is a matter of price. The price of oil from free flowing wells or pumped wells is so much below the cost of recovering oil from tar sands, or the cost of manufacturing oil by hydrogenation, that the latter are not within the economic realm.
As far as the Canadian situation is concerned. we are all feeling very much cheered by the recent discovery nt Leduc, Alberta. It
Supply-Mines and Resources

is believed' by those responsible for the development of that field that we may have in Canada, a very great field, one that within the coming year or two may produce oil sufficient to supply the prairie provinces, plus considerable quantities for delivery outside that area. That would be a great relief. The supply of oil to the prairie provinces has been increasingly difficult, as production in the Turner valley field has diminished. It is a relief to mow that our supply problem on the prairies may be taken care of. It will be a tremendous aelp if we have surplus oil from that area which can be either exported1 in exchange for oil delivered to eastern Canada or perhaps piped down, to eastern Canada for delivery direct.
Has the department kept in its own control the method that it promoted for taking oil out of the sand?
No. Any discoveries that we have made have been given freely to the industry. It is the business of the department to promote production and not to make money out of discoveries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On this same item may I ask the minister if he will make a statement regarding modern methods and devices of surveying the areas to determine mineral resources that might be located in them? I have in mind reports that are current about new ways of discovering rather quickly and easily whether there are valuable mineral resources underground. If he can add to that some remarks as to who is doing this in northern Canada and to what extent it is being done both by private industry and by his department, I should appreciate it. In asking for this statement I have in mind two points: first, the desire that we proceed with is much development as we can of the resources we have in northern Canada; second, the desire that the values which are there be conserved, so far as possible, for the Canadian people.

I assume that the device to which the hon. member refers is the flying magnetometer. It is more or less experimental in nature at the moment, but it does detect major changes in the structure of the earth and indicates areas which are likely to be mineralized. It is no more accurate than that, but it is a great help in exploring areas which can later be prospected more accurately. We have $30,000 in the estimates for experimental work on the flying magnetometer in Canada during the next current year. I might say that a licence has been issued to a United States firm which is doing work on the ftying magnetometer on the property of the Inter-
national Nickel Company. My deputy tells me that, there are three areas in Canada where work is being done. It is a means of prospecting which may turn out to be exceedingly important, and Canada expects to be in the forefront of the development.

This item provides $1,130,000 for the building of roads at Yellowknife. Will the minister give us some of the details with regard to the length of the roads, the type of road, who the contractor was, what the excavation was, whether the roads for this $1,130,000 are serviceable now, or whether they have been completed?

This road is being built by the province of Alberta, It is built under agreement with the Department of Mines and Resources. The problem is unique, in that the purpose of the road is to connect the highway system of Alberta with the Yellowknife area of the Northwest Territories. There are about three hundred miles in Alberta and about eighty miles in the Northwest Territories. The federal government is, of course, responsible for the full cost of building roads in the Northwest Territories; but owing to the importance of the road in opening up an important section of the Northwest Territories, the government agreed with the province of Alberta to pay at least half of the cost of the road in the province. I am told that this particular vote is for the road in the Northwest Territories. It is the full cost of the Northwest Territories section. In addition to that, we have an agreement with the province of Alberta to pay an amount which represents fifty per cent of the cost of the section of the road lying within Alberta, which is being built by the province of Alberta. I believe there is another vote for that. I have no information as to the contractor or the cost of the work.
What is the length of the road which is dealt with under this particular item?
Eighty miles.

Yes.

Has the British Columbia government nbtified the Department of Mines and Resources that it has $200,000 to spend on a road between Atlin and the Alaska highway? If it has so notified them, has it also asked them for the use of their machinery to work on that road?

The position is this. About half of this road is in the Northwest Territories and half of it is in British Columbia. The estimated cost of the road is about $600,000, being about $300,000 for the Northwest Territories part and about $300,000 for the British Columbia part. 15-i. Land registry, seed grain collections, administration of ordnance, admiralty and public lands, $91,940.

Before I say anything on this particular item, I wish to ask the minister a question. If he replies favourably, I shall not need to say any more. Is the government giving any consideration to cancelling the seed relief debts of from 1912 to 1919
and along about that time, which were incurred before there were other relief measures in the prairie provinces?

This is an old account dating from years away back when the government was in the seed grain business. All we are trying to do is to collect these accounts. It is an inactive branch of the department, except that we are owed this money and we should like to collect it.

That is, I am sorry to
say, the answer I expected to get.
What does it mean?

I wish the minister could have been a little bit more encouraging. I want to point out that these liens were taken against the land and sometimes-in fact, quite frequently-the land has changed hands. The present tenants, when they think they have the debt paid up now find that they actually have not, because in applying for their title they find they have quite a debt to pay. In the main I agree with the minister, that when a person contracts a debt he should pay it; 'but I know there have been occasions and circumstances when not only farmers but other people have been relieved of an old debt because of the passage of time and because of economic circumstances which have intervened between the time of the contracting of the debt and the present day.
I know the minister is acting on behalf of the other minister who is ill; and I am sorry that the regular minister is not here. I wish the present minister, who is doing a very good job, would give serious consideration to the matter. I want to give just one concrete case. I could give a great many, but I do not want to take up the time of the committee. The case I have in mind is that of the northeast quarter of section 16, township 28, west of the third meridian. Nearly thirty years ago, in 1918, this land was purchased, and at that time the principal amount owing was $465.90. As of January 8, 1947, the interest amounted to S740.50 making a total debt of $1,207.40. In this case the debtor has had a compromise offered by the department, in which compromise I have no doubt the department went as far as it had authority to go. That compromise offer was a cash settlement of $744.75. This piece of land is located in an area which is frequently subject to drought. Occasionally it gets a crop, but in the main one can say it just gets 'by. After a succession of bad years in the thirties, when we had both low prices and poor crops, people in that district
Supply-Mines and Resources

could not even get by and did anything and everything possible to get some little income on which to live.
A great many accounts are in a similar position. I have given what I think is a typical case. The man who owns this land has worked very hard. He has raised a large family and done a pretty good job as a citizen. Consequently I believe he should be relieved of this debt. He has done all the other things that have been, necessary to carry out his obligations. He has paid his municipal and school taxes; he has paid off his machinery debt, his mortgage and so on. He has paid the interest and all the rest of it, and finally he thought he was clear of debt and relieved of these obligations in his more than middle age. Then suddenly he found that, even under the compromise settlement, he still owed $744. That may not sound like a great deal of money to members of this house when they are dealing in these estimates with nothing less than a few thousand, which is just chicken feed, and on up into the millions; but it is a lot of money to struggle to pay after a lifetime of hard work. So I ask the minister to give serious consideration to instructing his department to cancel these debts. If these people are still involved it is because they have not been able to discharge these debts, no matter how hard they have tried. Other people,'such as the grocer and the machinery man, have accounted for their money up to the present. These people should be relieved of these debts now, because everything that could be done by the debtors has been done, and they should not have to continue to struggle to pay this money. I can appreciate the difficulties of trying to collect debts. I wish I could collect all those owing to me. I would be tickled to death and would offer an even better compromise than this on some of them. But I do not expect to collect, and I will not press for payment. I should like the government to be as lenient with those in difficult circumstances as I have been personally with some people in the same position, in a much smaller way but equally important. Will the minister give some serious thought to that suggestion?

I would point out to my hon. friend that there is a debt adjustment board in every province, made up of citizens of that province who in each case know the debtor and are sympathetic toward his problems. Adjustments are being made almost every day in connection with these loans, and I know of no case in which there has been absolute hardship on account of them. My hon. friend said they suddenly found themselves in debt. I think he will find that these debts go back

quite a number of years. The prairies were never so prosperous and the people of the prairies were never so well able to pay their debts as at the present time, due, I think in large part, to the careful administration of this government. We sincerely hope that in their days of prosperity they will liquidate these small debts and relieve the department of the necessity of dealing with these matters.

I cannot let it go quite as easily as that, though I do not suppose I can change the minister's mind. He may think he has said something fairly wise, but it is not quite so wise as one might expect from a man in his position and with his capabilities. When I said these people suddenly discovered themselves in debt I meant exactly what I said. Many of them did not know or had forgotten the loans were there. They had1 struggled through the years to provide the minimum necessities, and they thought they were clear; then they found they were not.
The minister said the prairies were never better off than they are at the present time. I am not going to dispute that statement; probably it is true. But when one considers all the years they were so badly off, to be a little better off now may not mean a great deal. A person in the gutter, hungry and broke, is better off if someone gives him a cup of coffee and a couple of doughnuts, but that is not good enough. A great many more years of prosperity-and I agree it will have to be in spite of the government over there -will be required before we can say the prairies are really well off. It is true that they are better off than they were and that they have paid some of their debts. Here is a deibt, however, that many of them have not been able to pay. I am sure, if the minister were dealing with these matters on a purely personal basis or as the manager of a concern he would give them a great deal more consideration than he appears to want to give them at the present time. As the head of a department representing the people of this country, I believe those he represents would appreciate it if he extended the same leniency to these people as I am sure he would if he were the manager of a business with which people were involved in this way, and in which he had come out so well.
It is all very well to say the farmers were never better off than they are now. I would remind the committee of what the Minister of Finance said in presenting his budget speech, that never in the history of Canada had the people such a surplus. Therefore we are all better off than we have ever been before. That goes for all the people. A great many

accounts have been cancelled, and I think these small accounts could be cancelled as well without the financial situation of Canada being affected.

156. Administration of Migratory Birds Convention Act, $57,100.

What measures are being taken to preserve the duck population of Canada? In a recent publication of the Ontario department of lands and forests it is stated that in 1943 our duck population was
145,000.000, and in 1946 it was only 80.000,000. From that it would look as though our ducks were being seriously depleted. What steps are being taken under this act to preserve this population? I should like to know also if Cuba has entered into an agreement under the Migratory Birds Convention Act?

We are faced with a difficult situation, due to the startling reduction in the known migratory waterfowl population on this continent. For the past two years, various adverse natural factors operating in Canada and in the United States have decimated the waterfowl to such an extent that increasing numbers of hunters have killed more ducks than were produced. The breeding stock has been cut into seriously.
This subject was probably the most important discussed at the provincial-dominion wildlife conference in February last, when topranking wildlife officials from all the provinces, and from the United States, presented the results of their surveys. It was agreed by all who were familiar with the situation that, unless the harvest of waterfowl in 1947 is greatly curtailed, this season may witness the collapse of this great sport. Some authorities have recommended a completely closed season until improved conditions permit restoration of a normal duck population.
In dealing with this situation on this side of the line the dominion, as the authority charged with responsibility for the administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, collaborates with the provinces which are responsible for the wildlife and, by consultation and exchange of information, it is possible to arrive at dominion and provincial regulations which are identical. Before the regulations are promulgated in Canada, we usually know what action is being taken on the United States side of the line. For a number of reasons, the conditions imposed there are always more drastic than those imposed in Canada. We do not know yet whether the' United States will have an open season for migratory birds this year. In Canada it seems likely that we shall have a short open season with greatly reduced bag limits.

I am given to understand that the slaughter of canvasback ducks in Cuba

Supply-Mines and Resources
is terrific during the tourist season because of the great influx of hunters. Then United States hunters are coming into Canada. This same article from the Ontario lands and forests departmental publication states that more birds were exported on ice than migrated on the wing. It would seem that something will have to be done when there has been a drop from 145,000,000 to 80.000,000 within two years and with additional hunters coming into the country. If not, we are going to lose this great game sport of wild duck hunting.

I agree that the situation is terrible. At least we are aware of the situation and will take steps. My hon. friend will appreciate the desirability of working along with the United States. I am sorry I have no information as far as the situation in Cuba is concerned.

make the request for some similar expenditures on the Fraser and Thompson rivers system. I have pressed for a similar survey of all that area as an integrated project.
