177. Branch administration, $92,371.

I was attempting to speak on this item this afternoon. At that time I reported the fact that there exists in Canada a situation of which a good many Canadians are not fully aware. I am referring to about 132,000 of the native inhabitants of this continent, the North American Indians, who in Canada are undoubtedly suffering wrongs and are denied certain human rights that we consider an essential part of the existence of every human being. Because of Canada's reputation in this matter, I think it is well that the department which has this responsibility should understand that this is not just a technical job; it is a job of rescuing a race of people who, I am convinced, have been seriously wronged. I am convinced that the Canadian Indian could be restored to a position of dignity and pride. My experience with these people, in studying and working with them, has convinced me that they have many fine characteristics which, if properly developed, could make a splendid contribution to Canada. The Indian people have been subjected to a term in reserves which has degraded and relegated them to a position of inferiority and almost to a position of dependence, such as might well be meted out to pariahs .who have become outcasts from society. That is not good enough.
The thing that stirs me about this is the fact that the whole thing is unnecessary. Some years ago the LTnited States took hold of this situation and has already made great strides in restoring these people. The New Zealand people, by their treatment of the Maoris, have rescued a very fine race of people who are making a splendid contribution to. that country. I am somewhat discouraged at times in speaking to the people of Canada, and to officials of the department, who refer to the Indian as a useless, lazy chap who will not work. That is not true. Medical men who have, made a study of the situation among our Indians have come to the conclusion that our Indian is a sick man.
The responsibility for the welfare of the Indian has been placed upon this government.

Sup-ply-Mines and Resources
and particularly upon this department. I am making a special plea, because I think there is a challenge here for officials in this department, to go out and rescue, a race of people who have been seriously wronged by the administration of Canada in the past. I am sure the Canadian people would not permit the condition which exists to continue to exist if they were aware of it. The fact that we have finally set up a committee of this house, which has been sitting for the past two years and which tabled its report the other day, reveals that the Canadian people are at least becoming aware of a tremendous responsibility in this field. That committee has found that there are conditions existing which they had not dreamed of before. I have been pleased with the attitude of the members of that committee toward this Indian problem. There seems to be an earnest desire on the part of many hon. members to do a real job of restoring these people. There is extensive want among these people; there is a neglect of the ordinary human needs. The rights of the Indian have been denied to him. He is placed in a position of dependence. He is not allowed to develop any of his talents m a private way. He is given no rights with regard to government or control of his own affairs. He is placed under the direction and control of an Indian agent. Often these Indian agents are unqualified with regard to any scholastic ability, and I am sure that in many cases their attitude with regard to the Indian is altogether wrong. The Indians are resentful of the treatment which they have had, but they have no redress; they have no avenue of approach to get redress for their grievances.
One of the greatest functions which this committee has performed in the past two years is that of being a sort of court of appeal to which these people could come and submit their grievances and, for the first time in a long time, inform the government of this country and the members of parliament oi some terrible conditions which exist. If you will go back over your history, Mr. Chairman, you will find that the Canadian government made treaties with these people. Treaties were made with the Indians of this country before it was British territory. After the British came, they made treaties with these Indians. Evidence was presented before that committee to the effect that those treaties have been broken and that the promises which were made to these Indians have not been fulfilled. Hundreds of treaties with these people were signed. They had faith in the government officials and the officials of the Queen when the promises were made. Now 'hey have no way of forcing the government's
hand. They have no way of compelling the government to fulfil its obligations. The condition of neglect which many of them are in is disgraceful. The living conditions in some of these reserves are deplorable. Medical attention had fallen to a low ebb. One of the good things this committee did was, I believe, to awaken the officials of the department to a realization that something was wrong. The committee has been pleased to notice that, in recent months, the government has taken hold of this matter of the health and welfare of the Indians and placed it under another department, and is spending a considerable amount of money in attacking the situation. But something will have to be done and done quickly. We cannot neglect the problem.
Among the recommendations which the committee handed down to the house yesterday was No. 2, which reads as follows:
That a commission in the nature of a claims commission be set up with the least possible delay to inquire into the terms of all Indian treaties, in order to discover and determine such rights and obligations as may herein be involved (or any subsequent substitution therefor) and to appraise and settle in a just and equitable manner any claims or grievances arising thereunder.
That is a valuable recommendation. The Indian people have lost faith in the white man. The Indian is distrustful of him. He resents his treatment, and you can hardly blame him when you go over the record of the department. Reserves were set aside, but we find that these reserves are being infiltrated by white people. Valuable property is being taken away from the Indians. Sometimes the band has consented and sometimes it has not. Proper records are not kept. In the matter of education and training there is a great deal which must be done. One of the Indian delegates who appeared before our committee said this: "The measure of the democracy of any nation may be judged by the measure of democracy it allowis its smallest minority to enjoy." These 132,000 people are enjoying no democracy. Canada is making itself liable to charges in the united nations council as a result of the way in which it treats a minority people of a different race within its own borders. That is how serious the situation is. If our treatment of these Indian people is the scale upon which we are to judge democracy in Canada, then Canada stands low indeed.
My plea with the government is for them to see that the commission recommended by t.he committee is set up. I should like to see upon that commission a representative of the
Supply-Mines and Resources

Indian race chosen by the Indians themselves. Of recent years the Indians are beginning to organize, but they have been left illiterate. They were supposed to be 'trained. The educational system among our Indians has fallen down miserably. The evidence given by government officials shows that there were
12,000	Indians in Canada who had no opportunity of any education whatsoever. How can you make a race of people with the situation like that? Education is a fundamental and basic thing upon which we must build these people if we are to make anything at all of them. They are largely illiterate. They have no power or ability to speak for themselves. They do not understand organization. They have often been fooled and tricked, and they have no avenue of redress; as a result, they are sinking into hopelessness. There was plenty of evidence, however, that certain groups- and I am speaking of agencies such as the Caughnawaga, the Six Nations at Brantford, a few of the Blackfeet Indians in Alberta and some of the Haida Indians on the western coast-had been able to achieve some possibility of progress. Those Indians showed remarkable characteristics and remarkable ability.
And the Moraviantown Indians.

Yes. The capacity is there, but the treatment of these Indians by the administrations of this country has been such as to keep them submerged and inferior. They are people with great possibilities.
My main theme is this: give these people a chance. Give them the ordinary fundamental human rights which should be allowed to every human being and you will be repaid a thousand-fold. The disgraceful conditions which have existed, and which exist today- even this very day-in spite of what has been done, are something of which Canadians cannot be proud. With some restoration of the ordinary rights of human beings, with some part in control and some responsibility with regard to the administration of their own affairs, even within their own little bands on their own reserves, and with some opportunity to train themselves, I am sure the results will be good. The Indians who have been taken off our reserves or who volunteered in the forces, and who went out and got proper medical care and proper food, made splendid records for themselves. However, when they come back to the reserves they find themselves relegated to positions of inferiority, and they deeply resent that.
I think it will also be found that when Canada made her treaties with the Indians

she promised them certain rights with regard to natural resources in the areas of land of the dominion. But when the dominion handed over the natural resources to the provinces, the Indians' rights were forgotten. The provincial governments do not recognize responsibility toward the Indians; that is a federal affair. There is a division of authority. I will say this, though. There has been some promise since this committee was formed two years ago. There are signs that officers of the department are awakening. I think the acting minister, in carrying on the job for the Minister of Mines and Resources who is ill, is doing fine work, and is doing the best he can. It is not easy for an engineer to act as a wet nurse, and the job is somewhat strange to him. I hope he will carry these recommendations on to the minister who, we hope, will soon be restored to health. There is a great job to be done. The committee which brought these recommendations down did all that it could do. But the recommendations are not being acted upon. This house passed resolutions saying that they were willing to support a proposal that old age pensions should be given to Indians on the reserves. I have seen conditions among the old people on the reserves, in places like Norway House, which are a disgrace to any people. The aged, the infirm and the blind on our reserves are suffering inhuman treatment or lack of treatment. This condition must be remedied.
I hope that every hon. member of the House of Commons will read the reports of the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate on the amendments to the Indian Act. A great deal of information has been obtained, and I want to thank a few of the newspapers across this country which have given of their space to tell the story of the Indians in Canada. A great deal is yet to be done, and I should like to have some report from the government as to whether or not they intend to set up this claims commission, and whether their plans are to give greater opportunity to the Indians to go out and make use of their capacities and abilities to further enrich Canada.

I would not want to detract from the speech of the hon. member, because I think I would agree with most of it, but he said that treaties made with the Indians in times past have been broken. Will he not agree that, while that may have been so in some particulars, those treaties have been added to and replaced to a great extent, with the result that the Indian has been getting much more than was provided in the treaties?

Mr. CASTLE-DEN: In some instances and under some treaties there have been some advantages; but I would say none of the advantages given the Indian in this way would recompense him for the loss he has suffered by being relegated to a position of inferiority. I suppose most of the treaties have been fulfilled to some extent, and many of them have been changed, but the thing the Indian does not like is the fact that he is placed in a position where he has no voice in regard to the changing of those conditions. Claims are settled without the Indian being consulted. Things are done with his lands, his reserves, without the Indian being asked. I referred to the fact that many of his rights were forgotten entirely when the natural resources of Canada were handed over to the provinces. At that time proper provision was not made for what he thought -were his inherent rights under the treaties which he, as a poor savage, sighed with the sophisticated people who had' everything on their side, including the fact that the treaties were in their language. Certainly the Indians of today have shown great willingness to come to an agreement with the government, and they are willing to help.

Since you have stated there should be an Indian on the proposed claims commission, with which I heartily agree, in view of the fact that we have not been able to get the Indians at our committee meetings to agree among themselves as to who should represent them, could you tell us how we should go about getting them to agree on an Indian to represent them on the claims commission?

Yes, gladly. If some little effort had been made by the government and others to get the Indians of Canada organized I am quite sure their good judgment would bring out fine men. If in a few months most of the provinces can gather together and organize the Indians to choose representatives-
Then would you tell me-
Just wait till I finish.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. All questions must be addressed to the Chair. I do not think it helps matters when hon. members discuss these matters between themselves.

I quite agree, Mr. Chairman. I was just about to say that in those areas where the Indians were assisted in getting together and organizing they were able to choose satisfactory representatives to appear before the committee. I am quite 83166-350
sure that when al'l the Indians of Canada become organized so that they can speak with one voice, they will choose good men. Their ability to tell their story and the way they told it showed what the Indians of this country can do.

I could probably stand here and1 talk for two or three hours on the wrongs andl troubles of the Indians of Canada, but I had rather hoped that, in view of the deliberations of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Indian Act, we would have very little, if any, discussion this session on- the estimates of the Indian department. Holding that view, I did not prepare, or anticipate making, any long speech on the Indian question. However I should like to say- it seems to me that the joint committee now considering this matter is carrying out its work in a just, reasonable and impartial manner. As I say, I could speak for hours on- the way I think the Indians have been ill-treated, but I believe, instead of getting into arguments, instead of discussing particular cases, instead of debating the general question of how the Indians have been treated, we should wait until the committee has finished its deliberations.
Hear, hear.

I hear some hon. members on the government side saying "hear, hear", and apart from any other consideration, probably they are well advised in doing so, in view of the fact that the present government has been in power for some twenty odd years out of the last twenty-five. As a matter of fact, the Indian problem has been on our hands since confederation, and every government that has been in power in this country must bear a certain amount of responsibility for the fact that our Indians have not been well and reasonably treated. Under no circumstances should the Indian question get down to a party level, or the level, of what this government has done, what that government has done, or what the other government has done. We should consider it on the basis of what will be best for the Indians and for Canada. Since the entire question is being fairly exhaustively considered at the present time by the joint committee, and since I believe it is anticipated their deliberations will continue next session, personally I would be in favour of passing the estimates of the Indian department at the present time and waiting for the results of the deliberations of the committee before embarking upon a debate which would more or less crystallize the views of the various groups in this parliament as far as the Indians are concerned.

I had not intended saying anything on this matter, because the committee has not yet formulated its recommendations or revised the Indian Act, and I-consider it premature to deal with what may be proposed to be done. However I am happy that the department is increasing the amount of these1 votes, particularly in the supplementaries. It is the first occasion for some time that this has been done, and I am glad to say the present Minister of Mines and Resources, the hon. member for Marquette, who is away because of illness, has been very sympathetic to the matter of improving the lot of the Indians. I say humbly that I was one who, more than ten years ago, or perhaps fifteen years ago-and I do not know anyone else who did-after making many surveys of Indian reservations myself, suggested that we set up a royal commission to investigate the whole problem of Indian administration. However, that did not take place. Indeed, nothing happened along that line until the present minister took office, at which time an attempt was made to improve the lot of the Indians by setting up the Indian Act committee.
I am not going to say anything about the work of the committee, because in my judgment it would be premature to do so at the present time. However I am pleased to see an increase in the estimates for this purpose, and I am hopeful that next year we shall see results, and that at the next session the act may be revised and a full programme set out for the benefit of the Indians. At that time I shall have something further to say about Indian affairs.

May I associate myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Yorkton. The past his. tory of our treatment of Indians does not make good reading. I believe we may accept the fact that today we are making efforts to do something better for them.
As one who has spoken on the same subject in the house before, and as one who has spent some years on Indian reserves, I should not like the impression to go out from the committee that all who have had anything to do with Indians in the past have sought to exploit them or to cause their downfall. Rather I would pay tribute to many hundreds of fine men and women of all Christian denominations who have spent many of the best years of their lives in seeking to improve the lives of the Canadian Indians. I feel that much has been accomplished by these people, and that, as a result of the fine work done on many of those reserves, we have cause to look forward to the future with great hope.
May I also express my appreciation of the

work done by the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in regard to this matter of revising the Indian Act. I am sorry I was not privileged to be a member of the committee, but I have followed its work with interest. Like many thousands of others,
I am waiting for the official report of the committee to see what improvements will be made in the Indian Act and what sort of future lies ahead of the Indian people.
Reference has been made to the outstanding ability shown by delegations from the east and the west before the committee. That exhibition of ability can be duplicated throughout the Indian population. Many of our Indians today are every bit as worthy^ of trust as are many of our white population, if we would only give the Indians the opportunity.
I should like to say something further about the development of native handicrafts, which perhaps might more properly be discussed under a later item. That' is one phase of Indian life which should be fully developed. The Indians of Canada have developed some excellent handicrafts, and they should be perpetuated. It would be a great mistake to allow those handicrafts to die out. The time is ripe to give the younger people on the reserves training in the handicrafts of their fathers and mothers, so that these exhibitions of native skill may not be lost.
I hope that the work of the committee, which is being brought more closely to the attention of the people of Canada, may result in a new and better day for our Canadian Indians.
How many teachers does the department employ in residential and) day schools of Indians in Canada?

The department employs more than 300 teachers in day schools. The churches employ the teachers in the residential schools, of which I believe there are about eighty. I cannot say how many teachers are employed per school, but I should think that would depend upon the size of the school.

There has been some question as to whether the teachers are fully qualified and have certificates from the provinces in which they are employed. How many of these are qualified teachers, and how many hold Canadian qualifications? I understand that some have qualifications from the United Kingdom, and1 some from the United States. I was promised a break-down in committee, but I did not receive it.

Some of the teache-rs are not fully qualified, but the department is striving to raise the standard. All we can do is to report progress and continue efforts in that direction.

I should like to speak briefly about contracts entered into by employers with persons from displaced persons camps. Some time ago I placed a question on the order paper. It was later passed as an order for return, and I received the return yesterday. I find that a large number of companies have made application for persons from displaced persons camps. The return before me shows applications from thirty-eight different companies. The Canadian lumber industry has made applications on behalf of fifteen companies.
I wTish to refer particularly to a contract set out in another return tabled this morning. This form of contract is that of the Great Lakes Paper Company with the individual displaced persons who will be taken to Canada. I regret very much that in industries where there are labour organizations which have agreements with employers, no effort has been made to get the employers and trade unions together with respect to these contracts. I am satisfied that the method followed will not result either in good relationships between the persons brought in and the company, or in good relationships with other employees of the company.
The agreement I have before me is between the Great Lakes Paper Company Limited of Fort William, which in the agreement is named as the employer-and then there is a place for the name of the individual employee. The first section in the agreement reads:
>1. The employer agrees to employ the employee in lumbering, pulpwood or logging work for a period of ten months to run from the date the employee begins work on the operations of the employer.
I do not believe that an agreement should be made for as short a period as ten months. If you are only going to make an agreement for ten months you may just as well bring these people here and let them find their owni employment. An employee who has worked for only ten months will not have earned any benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and if his employment terminates at that time he will not be eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits. A contract should not be made for less than 83166-3501
two years, and any employer who cannot guarantee work for two years should not apply for people of this kind.
In the case of the Dionne labour my hon. friend's leader said that a con-traat for two years represented slavery. It is hard to satisfy my hon. friend.
It is not hard to satisfy either my leader or myself. When the leader of our party was referring bo the Dionne case he was referring ot the terms of the contract, not to the period of the contract.

speechtext: To the time.

That was the objection there. I am objecting to contracts in any event, because bringing contract labour to this country is contrary to our laws, but if we are to have contract labour the period of employment should be longer than ten months. The second section reads:
2. The employer agrees to pay wages to the employee during the currency of this agreement at the rate and in the manner prevailing in the locality for comparable classifications of employment.
If organized labour in the industry has an agreement with the employer, then the terms in the contract providing for wages and conditions of work should be those provided by that agreement. As far as I know, the employees in all these industries are organized, but there may be some where they are not. Wherever -they are organized' there are agreements. The wages paid under such agreements and those paid in industries where labour -is unorganized may not be the same. Under this agreement the employer is not bound to -pay the wages in effect in his own industry. He agrees to pay the prevailing wages in the locality. If there is a difference between the wages paid in the industry and the rates in the locality you are going to have immediate conflict.
I regret exceedingly that the government did not insist that representatives of the workers in industries where they are -organized are associated with the agreement. If we are to brin-g these people here -they should be brought in on a basis where there will not be exploitation, or at least where the exploitation will be kept to a minimum.
I remember what happened in this country after the first world war. When labour was scarce during the war the workers in the lumber industry were able to organize and to improve their conditions of work which had been very bad. When the war ended, employers took advantage of the situation that developed. Even though their camps were

not operating, when they found that workers were being taken from all parts of Canada to the harvest fields in the west they made application to the labour exchanges for workers for their lumber camps. Of course there were no workers available, and then they asked permission to bring in workers from Europe. Workers came in from Europe and, not knowing the conditions in the industry, they were used to destroy conditions that had been built up with a great deal of effort.
I do not want the country to go through the same process again, because it does not make for good labour relations. It does not make for peace in the industry, and it does not make for good relations as between unorganized and organized workers in the same industry. I should like the Acting Minister of Mines and Resources and the Minister of Labour, who, I believe, has been consulted in this matter, to get together and, wherever possible, insist that there be some contact between the organized workers in the industry and the employers, should any arrangements of this kind be made in the future.

This matter has been mentioned several times, so that I shall not speak about it tonight, but I should like the minister to give a specific answer to this question: When will it be possible to investigate cases of people who are now classified as enemy aliens in order to determine whether they are really enemy aliens? I referred to a case of this kind this afternoon. This man used to reside in Roumania and his family was put in a concentration camp where some of them were killed. He is now a Canadian and wants to bring them to this country, but they are classified as enemy aliens. Obviously they were not, because it was thought necessary by the enemy to put them in this camp. When I asked an explanation of the department all they could say is that they have not found it possible to establish an inspectional staff. When can these people hope to be able to enter Canada?

The department is continually faced with the problem of getting in touch with these persons. The rule is that if the person in question was opposed to the enemy government he is admissible, provided that he can get to a place where the department can function. Nothing can be done as far as real enemy aliens are concerned until they cease to be enemy

aliens. 1 presume that, after the peace treaties are signed and ratifications are exchanged, the government will no longer regard them as enemy aliens. In the meantime it is necessary for a man of an enemy country to prove that he was opposed to an enemy government in order to be admissible at this time.
Is any procedure laid down governing these cases?

Each case is judged on its merits. The investigation is in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who have their contacts in these countries. If it can be shown in an individual case that a family was killed off because of resistance to an enemy power, the man W'ould be admitted. The onus of proof is on the man to show that he was not an enemy alien. If he had lived in an enemy country the presumption w'ould be that he was an enemy alien. If he can prove otherwise he is admissible.

In Switzerland or in a country where there are no inspectional facilities at the moment, are people free to leave that country and go elsewhere where there are inspectional facilities and be examined there?
It depends on the laws of their own country.
But so far as Canada is concerned?
Yes. If they turned up in Switzerland and could be examined there, and there was the necessary proof, they would be admitted to Canada. We inspect them wherever we find them.

I grant that the subject of immigration has been thoroughly discussed today and on other occasions in the house. I simply want to say I listened with great interest to what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Dauphin, and while I may be taking some risk because he sits opposite to me in this house I should like to say that I am in substantial agreement with the remarks he made. We should try to reconcile the moves that are made under industrial orders in council with the applications that have been made by Canadians for the entry to Canada of their relatives, and I hope that the representatives of the immigration branch will take to heart what the hon. member for Dauphin said. Some certificate or document should be placed in the hands of relatives of Canadians who reside in displaced persons camps, so that when some shipping movement is made such as was made in the past for Polish soldiers, and as will be made in the future for industrial workers, these relatives of Canadians would get some preference over others in the camps in that they are related to Canadians.
If I might have the permission of the committee, I should like to say, with respect to item 185, that I personally have the feeling that there is something inequitable in the rigidity of the present order in council which says that the child in China of a Canadian citizen must, be under the age of eighteen to be admitted to Canada. I know that this subject has been debated thoroughly in the house, and I have a great deal of sympathy for the arguments that have been presented pro and con, and I feel that all arguments of humanity are against the rigidity which says you should divide a family, when, for instance, an unmarried daughter nineteen years of age is refused admission to Canada to join her father in this country and an unmarried daughter under eighteen may be admitted. I want to lodge my protest against this order fixed as it is. I think the humane attitude would be that the department should amend the order in council at least to give discretion
to the officials to admit the unmarried daughter of a Canadian citizen from China to Canada.

The prosecution of anything in the nature of a national parks policy has been altogether without imagination. I am not reflecting on this government; I am reflecting on the entire policy as it has been carried on by all governments. I do not think it is due to the permanent officials. I am sure they would be delighted to make our parks the best in the world. What I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, is that the department, either as a government enterprise or in conjunction with private individuals, many of whom would be only too anxious to cooperate, should provide in our national parks-I refer particularly to Banff, Jasper, and Waterton, which I know best-accommodation which the ordinary citizen could afford to occupy. The unfortunate fact is that our so-called national playgrounds are not within the reach of the purse of the ordinary citizen of this country. The existence at Banff, at Jasper and at lake Louise of luxury hotels is an excellent thing and is bringing a lot of United States tourist money into this country. At the same time, in these parks we should have accommodation which would be within the reach of all our citizens. I have spoken on this matter before in the
Supply-Mines and Resources

house. The solution of it is so easy that I am sorry it has not been reached before.
When I was in Yellowstone national park the year before the war broke out, in 1938, I saw there large numbers of what might be called tourist cabins, accommodation to the lowest purse, composed of slabs of trees sawn off and made into cabins, with a covered space for a man to put his car underneath and with practically nothing in them except a bed without, of course, any bedding on it. You could rent these for seventy-five cents a night. This meant that almost any individual could go to Yellowstone national park with his family and rent one or two, or whatever his requirements were, of these, and the price was within his reach. Unfortunately, in our national parks we have nothing along that line. I would seriously suggest to the acting minister that steps be taken immediately to build in our national parks something comparable with the sort of thing I have described, which existed as long ago as 1938 in Yellowstone park in the United States, so that people of moderate means who wished to spend their holiday in these parks would be able to get accommodation within their reach.
The greatest weakness in our national parks is that there does not exist in them accommodation at a reasonable and cheap rate, so that our own people could go there and enjoy the beauties and the pleasures of these playgrounds. Personally I feel very strongly about this. I think our parks are the best in the world. I do not think any country has anything which can even approach Banff, Jasper and Waterton national parks. We have an asset there, the value of which the great majority of our people do not realize. At least we should take these minimum steps to make it available to our own people.
The second thing I should like to bring out in order to develop these parks, to get a large amount of tourist traffic from our own people and from the people of the United States, a long series of riding and hiking trails should be constructed for the summer time. It would mot coat much money and it would produce a great deal of added interest and traffic to the parks. So far as winter is concerned, many of these same trails could be used as ski trails. In addition, there needs to be built a considerable number of ski trails which will take advantage of the high hills and the long continued snow which lasts in a large area of these national parks until well on into May and June. That also would attract a large number of skiers. Nearly everyone will

recognize that skiing is a constantly increasing popular sport, and the development of these parks as skiinig grounds would mean a large increase in the winter tourist traffic to this country. At the present time our tourist traffic is almost entirely summer traffic. If we could develop in Canada skiing resorts to which people could go without having to spend too much money-and Canada has certainly some of the best skiing country in the world-we would help the entire national economy. I would ask the acting minister and this branch of the Department of Mines and Resources to give the most earnest consideration to carrying out these two suggestions, cheaper accommodation the year around in the parks, and the provision of hiking and trail riding facilities in the summer andi skiing trails in the winter, which will bring people to our parks.

Earlier this evening I was asking the minister about the road programme in the national parks. I should like to observe here that for the whole of this session I have had a resolution standing on the order paper with regard to a trans-Canada highways programme on the part of the federal government, or rather the desirability of developing such a programme. Opportunity has not been given to discuss it at this session. S5i. Grant to the Royal Society of Canada, $4,500.

I am not disapproving
the grant to the Royal Society of Canada. They do excellent work. I know of the lectures they provide and the information service which they supply, but I should like a little further information as to the reasons for this grant and what it is being used for.

This grant has been in the
estimates of the national research council for at least the last ten years. I understand that it is by arrangement between the council and the society.
I know it is an old grant, but I should like to know whether the royal society uses it for travelling expenses, lectures, or a definite work of any kind.
I think it is just a sustaining grant which goes into the general funds.

Will the minister say
whether this is the only grant?
No.
I think another grant is made by the government to the royal society. Possibly the minister can say this is the only one he knows of.
This is the only one I know of.

The hon. member for
York West said that the society does a useful work. I shall display my ignorance and ask what work it does. Unless I get an answer, I shall remain in ignorance, which will not be good for the committee or myself.

All I can say is that the members of the royal society are the most distinguished scientists of Canada. They publish papers. It is considered! the highest honour that can come to a scientist to be appointed to the royal society. I believe it is worth while as a forum and for the recognition of scientists in general.	[DOT]
The royal society's interest extends beyond what is properly known as science. I think it goes into art, music, literature and the whole sphere of cultural life.
I know it gives lectures in Toronto every so often on scientific and research effort. I should like to know what else it does.

Item agreed to.
